subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just previous to the adjournment of the House on Friday night I had offered to the Minister of Finance my very sincere congratulations on the manner in which he had delivered the budget speech some three weeks previously. It was with a great deal of pleasure that I was able to do this. I must confess to him to-day, however, that it is with equal sorrow I find myself not able to follow him into the promised land to which the singularly wonderful budget delivered by him holds out the prospect of leading us. I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman himself is really none too sanguine in his expectations despite his rosy anticipations. The Finance Minister talked to us in terms of millions. He referred to the imports and exports, to the balance of trade, to the reduced taxation which he claimed has been brought about, and to the improvement in the railway situation and the figures he used were up in the millions. I cannot help thinking that while these figures sound good they are of little interest to the ordinary citizen 
of this Dominion. In this country the great percentage of our population is really struggling to make a living and is not interested in the millions spoken of by the Minister of Finance. That hon. gentleman would have us believe that prosperity is right upon us, and that Canada is prospering to-day as she never did before. Yet deep down in his own heart, and deep down in the hearts of all those hon. gentlemen who uphold him in his argument, they must admit that at every street or crossroads comer in city, town, hamlet or country place the same old lament is heard, " Times are hard, and money is hard to get." That is the condition which exists throughout Canada at the present time. I have sat in this House ever since January 7th last, and every day there has been a sitting I have heard a cry of despair go up from some hon. member or from the representative of a particular section in this Dominion. Yet it is said we have prosperity in Canada.
Conditions in the west have been spoken of. We all agree that there are some conditions there which can and ought to be remedied. We all agree that the people of the west are not as prosperous as the Minister of Finance would lead us to believe. What did we find within the last year and a half? That actually, because of the gloomy outlook, some outstanding men in the west were talking of secession, of separating from the eastern part of Canada. Why should that be, if conditions are so prosperous as they say? But Mr. Speaker, if. we go into the west we find millions and millions of acres of soil possessing sufficient fertility to produce vegetation of all kinds in abundance and a sturdy race of men and hardy women, who are not indolent, but who are toiling to build up that great country and to provide a heritage for those who will follow them. Why should these men talk secession, if they are prosperous?
Let us look into conditions in the Maritime provinces. Y'ou know Mr. Speaker, that member after member from that section of the House has been on his feet day after day telling us of the needs, the wants and the wrongs of those eastern provinces. We do not have to take the word even of these hon. gentlemen. We all recollect what occurred in the House not more than a year ago. We all remember that a certain industrial condition existed down there which cost the lives of human beings. You will remember that in connection with the industrial unrest in. Nova Scotia human lives were sacrificed. Human blood was shed. Why? Because they were prosperous? Not at all. It was-

The Budget-Mr. Maloney
because of industrial conditions which existed then and which exist to-day and which will continue to exist as long as we live under the same system of government as we have in this House at the present time. What did % the government of Canada of that day do to remedy conditions in Nova Scotia? Did they do one single, solitary thing to help relieve the suffering miners and their families? Did they do anything to bring about better conditions in that section? They did nothing at all. Well, yes, they did one thing. They sent soldiers down there from Toronto and Kingston to shoot down if necessary a^y man who would raise a hand in defence of his starving wife or children.

speechtext:
When you send a soldier out on duty his orders are to shoot down men if necessary. I have touched upon conditions in the west. I have referred to the condition in the Maritime provinces. I will ask hon. members for a moment to come back to the central provinces and see what evidence of prosperity we find? You can go into town after town from one end of Ontario, or of Quebec, to the other, and you will find factory after factory with the doors securely locked. You will find man after man looking for work. Then go out into the country districts and you will find many farmers, at one time prosperous, who have abandoned their farms. You will see farm after farm abandoned. You will find farmer after farmer struggling to make a meagre existence, and yet they tell us we have prosperity in Canada.
In order to increase this wonderful prosperity the Minister of Finance has brought down his budget. Let us see what species of cure-all this budget is. It is not my intention to go into it at great length, but I will deal with the main item. We are told it is a poor man's budget-for the benefit of the poor man. We shall see. The first item of that budget, which perhaps is the most serious of all, is the one providing for a cut in the automobile tax. At one fell swoop the Minister of Finance cut the head off the most thriving industry in Canada, one of the best industries for the future of the country, and yet he tells us it is in the interest of the poor man. We all know the poor man does not owTn an automobile, and those of us who are foolish enough to own one, *even though we are poor, know that the amount saved by virtue of the reduction in the duty will mean very very little indeed. Why Mr. Ford in his price list just published claims a reduction of from $10 to $45 in the various models which he turns out. We know the average life of one of these cars with ordinary care is perhaps ten years. In other words we save from $1 to $5 a year on our car. Again that saving of from $1 to $5 a year you have the fact that the government, by virtue of this legislation, has jeopardized t'he position of 30,000 of our citizens, who are to-day engaged in the occupation of manufacturing and distributing automobiles. In addition to this 30,000 you have their dependents, numbering more than 125,000, whose living is jeopardized by this cut. Furthermore you strangle the industry, prevent its future development, but, greater than all, you weaken the confidence of investors in the fiscal future of the great Dominion of Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, we want cheaper automobiles. We all believe that to-day auto-

mobiles are selling at a price altogether too high, but is there no way in which a reduction of price might be [DOT] brought about, without strangling the industry, and injuring our fiscal .future? The thought occurred to me that if instead of cutting off or lowering the duty, as has been done, or will be done if the budget is passed, we raised the duty on all automobiles coming into Canada to such a height that the Canadiafi market would be preserved for the Canadian manufacturer, it would mean for them a larger market. Then after this tariff board has been fully authorized to do business, we might let them go down, examine the books and audit the accounts of the various automobile manufacturers and if necessary, set a reasonable price at which cars might be sold in Canada. If not, we could limit the profits which might be derived from the manufacture and sale of these cars. In that way automobiles might be sold much cheaper than under the present legislation while at the same time this industry would be encouraged and our fiscal interests preserved.
We are told that the income tax is another item in the budget affecting the poor man. We know that prior to this budget being thought of, a married man writh an income of $2,000 was exempt from this taxation. We do not consider that a man with a salary of $2,000 a year is a poor man; as a matter of face compared with many people in this country he is a rich man. In the year 1923 the farm labourers of the Dominion from coast to coast drew an average annual wage of $372 with board, or $611 without board, and employees in industrial establishments drew an average yearly salary of $937. In all, almost 500,000 Canadians were drawing an average salary of $800 a year. Will they call this a poor man's budget? What has the government done for the labourer by bringing down this budget change with regard to income tax? It has shifted the burden of our national debt from the shoulders of those who are most able to bear it to the people who are drawing salaries of less than $1,000 a year, and yet we are told that this is a poor man's budget.
The reduction in the postal rate from three cents to two cents was indeed a surprise. Nobody ever thought of it; there was no great desire on the part of the people of Canada for a reduction in postage. What does this reduction mean? It means a loss in revenue to the Post Office Department of $5,000,000 a year. It is to the credit of the Postmaster General and the splendid officers who are to-day working under him that the work they have been doing is so excellent

The Budget-Mr. Maloney
that their department is able to stand a reduction if this kind. If this reduction means a decrease in revenue of $5,000,000 for that department, what does it mean to the poor men of this country? The ordinary individual who is not doing business writes possibly fifty, sixty or seventy letters a year. The farmer, for example, may write fifty or seventy-five letters a year and he will therefore save fifty or seventy-five cents through this reduction; but what the farmer is more particularly anxious about to-day is not to save this fifty or seventy-five cents, but to have an improved mail service throughout the Dominion?
I say to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) who is supposed to be the leader of the farmers from the Atlantic to the Pacific: You are anxious for the comfort and welfare of those whom you are supposed to lead; if you are really desirous of making life on the farm more congenial for the boys and girls there, I would ask you to have the government remodel this item of legislation because you have the power to do that. Let them raise the postal rate again from two cents to three cents, and in doing so, save $5,000,000 to the revenue of this country. Then have the government spend that sum of $5,000,000 in extending the rural mail service through sections in your constituency, my constituency and every other rural riding from end to end of Canada.
The greatest boon to rural life in this country within the last half century has been the introduction of the rural mail. It is with great pride that I offer to you, Sir, as perhaps the father of that legislation, my most sincere congratulations, and I believe every citizen of Canada who enjoj's the benefit of the rural mail delivery will back me up in that statement. If the Minister of Finance is still determined to put two-cent postage into effect in this country I would ask him to consider the advisability of allowing us to use these two-cent postage stamps where today we have to employ a separate stamp, an inland revenue stamp. If this could be done it would materially simplify matters with business men and in addition it would help to make up in some small degree the loss of revenue which will ensue to the various postmasters throughout the Dominion by virtue of the change in the postal rate. I would be in the interest of the department and I believe it would bring in more money in the end.
I would like to refer for a moment to the question of old age pensions. It has been said that an offer, a gesture has been made. What has been the effect of that gesture? I
listened a few days ago to the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) referring to the hardy fishermen of the frozen northwestern boundary of his constituency. What a wonderful thing this pension would be for these men in their old age and their dependents? The government have made that gesture; they have raised the hopes of the aged from end to end of Canada; but when this bill becomes law. if it ever does, those hopes will be dashed to the ground because this legislation cannot become operative without the-consent of the provinces. They place so-much money in the hands of the provinces-and ask them to shoulder the balance and administer the law. Why should they place on the shoulders of the provinces this additional burden when already they are bowed down underneath loads of debt. I say to those self-constituted labour leaders of the city of Winnipeg:	If you believe that the
labouring classes are behind you in your desire for a system of old age pensions-and I believe they are-prevail upon the government to bring in a real old age pension law a pension to which they will contribute in its entirety irrespective and independent of all the provinces. If you will do that you will have behind you the support of seventy-five per cent of the membership of this House. While I do not like the legislation which has been introduced, while I do not believe it will ever come into effect in Ontario, or Quebec, or some of the other provinces, yet because of the fact that I am in favour of a system of old age pensions, I will support this legislation. We have heard a great deal in connection with the improvement in the railway situation in Canada. I could take you, Sir, into the county of Renfrew and show you how it is that the distinguished gentleman who presides over the destinies of the Canadian National rail-way system is able to produce a statement as good as the government claims it to be. In that particular district of the county of Renfrew, a thickly populated district front which during the last few years have gone-into the coffers of this government and the provincial government thousands and thousands of dollars of lumbering operations and other general business carried on in that section, I could show you two points a distance of fifty miles apart where it takes four days to make the round trip on the Canadian National railway. This has been brought about by the cutting down of the service

and no doubt this is typical of many other sections-to such a point that it is absolutely useless; we would be better without such a service at all if we could have these tracks

The Budget-Mr. Maloney
taken up and a good automobile road built throughout that district. If he has been following that plan throughout the country it is little wonder that expenses have come down, but when travelling from city to city in eastern Canada one does not see any evidence of anything of this kind. What one finds is one train trying to be better than another, and there is a multiplication of trains from day to day.
My hon. friends to my left have been promised many things by this government, and no doubt they have been assured that everything from their standpoint will be ideal in the days to come. I would ask my hon. friend from Brandon to take to heart the words of that old French poet:
Kings' promises are airy dreams
And scarcely la9t between the day's extremes.
The great trouble in Canada to-day is lack of stable government and the want of confidence on the part of the people in this adJ ministration. If there is one thing more than another that we require in this country it is a government in office such as the people can trust. But the government of the day, through its Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), has broken faith with the Canadian people. The right hon. gentleman broke faith with them in relation to his Richmond Hill speech, and again he has failed to keep the pledge he gave them in the Speech from the Throne. I say therefore that it is his duty to resign.

speechtext:
Canadian said some time ago that what Canada needed was a fiscal policy, relief frcm burdensome taxation and immigration. I believe that the reduction of $25,000,000 in these troublesome and burdensome taxes will make Canada a more attractive place to live in and will be a great step towards the realization of these three aims.
A good deal has been said since I came into this House as to the desirability of establishing industries. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) pointed out that St. Paul and Minneapolis had increased their population, providing a market for the farmers, to a much greater extent than had Regina, Swift Current, Moose Jaw and Prince Albert. Another hon. member argued that we should first build up the cities, and the rural communities would develop later. We tried that in the west, and if you go to any of the Canadian cities mentioned you will find a number of deserted, shut down and neglected factories. Medicine Hat is perhaps better endowed by nature as a manufacturing centre than any of these cities, but a number of industries have started and failed there. It was not a question of protection; it was not because of lack of capital; they failed because there was no market to absorb their product. These industries will be built up and will prosper some time, but not until the general development of the country provides a market for their products. You cannot build a tower without a foundation, and you cannot build an industrial city without a market.
Having in mind conditions as they actually exist, I believe we should trade with other countries in order to get a market for the products of our farms and factories. As a person uses six bushels of wheat a year, it would take about seventy million people to consume our surplus wheat production, and as a person uses sixty pounds of beef a year, it would be necessary to have thirty additional cities the size of Hamilton, Ontario, to consume the cattle exported last year.
It has been asked in this House why Canada should have a low tariff when every other country in the world has a high tariff. I do not believe all the people in the world are in favour of a high tariff. I have here a resolution which was passed unanimously by the Congress of International Chambers of Commerce at Brussels last year. At this congress were represented thirty-five nations, by their leading bankers and commercial magnates. The resolution is as follows:
The chamber has directed attention to interferences with the return of normal trade conditions and employment caused by artificial barriers, obstructive to intercourse between the nations, such as extreme tariffs, unreasonable customs regulations and 	,
restriction on transportation. All of these have the effect of increasing the delivered cost of goods and preventing the widest possible distribution and use of the world's products, which are the basis of better living standards and progress. The chamber appeals to the business men of all countries to study these questions, and to exert their influence for the removal, as promptly as possible, of all unnatural and uneconomic restrictions of this kind.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that agriculture is an industry which must be carried on with a very small margin of profit, and in the past the farmers have had to pay too much for the things they have had to buy. It has been stated in this House that prices may be low even though the tariff is high, but experience teaches us that the opposite is usually the case. There is not sufficient competition to assure us that the prices will be right if the tariff is very high, and although the last speaker referred to the possibility of fixing prices, no one has suggested any practical way by which the prices of the dozens of varieties, of the hundreds of articles used in this country could be fixed. It would therefore seem that the tariff is the best method of keeping prices low and preventing exploitation. A few articles may occasionally be sold at a low price if the tariff is high, but all articles must always be sold at the right price if the tariff is low because outside competition will force them to be sold at that price. Therefore, the first casualty resulting from putting on a high tariff would be the exhausting of the purchasing power of the people of the country and the stifling of the basic industries, and the second casualty would be the destruction of the market which the manufacturer had enjoyed for his goods.1* I have listened with a pretty open mind to the discussion which has taken place in this House, and I have heard it argued repeatedly that we are exporting raw materials and bringing back the finished products. I have looked up the records for 1914, 1922 and 1925, and this is what I find: Take our dealings with the Argentine republic, for instance. We exported manufactured goods as follows to the Argentine republic:
Exports to Argentine Republic

$ 293,900	Rubber goods	$1,234,0481,104,156	Agricultural implements	4,125,943470,291	Sewing machines	1,110,315558,389	Automobiles and	parts	2,242,906
Our total exports to the Argentine for 1922 amounted to $3,233,423, and for 1925 to $10,322,373, an increase in the three years of about $7,000,000. There were also other manufactured articles such as razors, iron pipe and tubing, nails, copper and structural steel that we exported.

The Budget-Mr. Gershaw
Now let us test it in another way. Take Italy, for example. We export a lot of flour to Italy. In 1925 we exported $514,660 of flour to Italy, or more than our total exports of all commodities to Italy in the year 1914, when hon. gentlemen opposite were shaping the destinies of this country. Our exports of fish, canned and dried, to Italy in 1925, amounted to $1,568,419, or three times the amount of our total exports of all commodities to Italy in 1914. Now I submit that if we found a market in Italy for fish to that extent, our fishermen were that much better off, because their purchasing power was increased, and as far as the manufacturer was concerned, it was better for him that we shipped this fish to Italy because thus the Canadian market for manufactured goods was enlarged, and the manufacturer found a larger market for the sale of his products.
We might follow this record of our increased trade through the entire list of countries with which we do business, and we will find exactly the same condition existing. Everywhere we are extending our markets for manufactured goods. The increase in the export of a few manufactured goods between the years 1922 and 1925 is shown as follows:
Manufactured Goods Exported
1922	1925
$4.061.S09	Rubber goods	$11,458,4585.345,308	Agricultural implements	11,342,712
If you take sewing machines, vehicles, including automobiles, razors, pig iron, and machinery other than agricultural implements- in all these cases you will find that our export of manufactured goods is rapidly and progressively increasing. This is good business for us because it helps to increase the purchasing power of the people of this country, just as the lowering of the tariff, which makes prices lower, helps to increase the purchasing power of the people.
During the election campaign last October our Conservative friends said that the Liberal policy was all	wrong. They said that we
were sending our raw products to the United States to be manufactured, and importing manufactured goods from that country. Since I have come to Ottawa I have taken the trouble to look up the United States Statistical Abstract and I find that the United States are shipping out a great deal of stuff in the raw or unmanufactured state, as follows: 1922	1925

You will note from these figures that the United States is sending out quite a bit of stuff in the form of raw material. You will
note also that she made a marked increase in the export of raw materials in 1925. Why do they do this? Every country in the world exports raw material, and they do it because it pays them to do it. Britain exports coal, and buys cotton; Canada exports wheat, and buys crude oil; the United States exports cotton, and buys wood and oil. Nations, protected or otherwise,	no matter what their
tariffs are, must trade with one another. Let us see what Canada is doing in this regard. The following table shows our exports to the United States for the years 1922 and 1925, in round figures:

You will notice that in the three years our exports to the United States increased by $125,000,000, and of this $32,000,000 was accounted for by raw materials, and $93,000,000 by the increase made in the export of manufactured, or partly manufactured, goods.
Some hon. gentleman opposite have said that they can see very few signs of prosperity in Canada. One hon. gentleman a short time ago mentioned the fact that prices of Canadian stocks and securities had risen very greatly since 1921, and some hon. gentleman opposite pointed out that that did not necessarily mean prosperity, that it might mean capital was very timid and that people wished to invest in these seasoned securities. I think there is very little to justify that view. In the Financial Times of May 7, 1926, I find this:
The gross earnings of 65 Canadian companies reveal an increase of $25,000,000 over those for 1924.
From a shareholder's point of view, the extent of the improvement is more exactly reflected by the improvement in average earnings on the common stocks of the companies under review. A gain of over 21 per cent on the average outstanding common capitalization is shown with earnings equivalent to an average of 11.5 per cent as compared with earnings equivalent to 8.9 per cent during the year 1924.
Surely if the stock of these companies is advancing so rapidly in price, and if they are able to show earnings of 11.5 per cent in 1925 as compared with 8.9 per cent in 1924, these large industrial concerns are doing fairly well and do not need the help which hon. gentlemen opposite would have us believe.
I believe that the budget will meet with the approval of the Canadian people because it is helping those who have the best right to that help, and I believe that it will not interfere with the prosperity of the large industrial concerns. I think that the policy behind this budget is one which is bringing about a fair share of prosperity, is bringing about national well-being, and above all, what

speechtext:
Mr Speaker, I desire in the first place, to assure my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that I regretted exceedingly not being able to be here to listen to his very interesting budget and to have a first hand opportunity of saying something about it. In the second place, I wish to thank the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) for the very excellent presentation he made and the criticism which he gave of the budget, a criticism which has never yet been answered. I gaze upon the Finance Minister with absolute amazement to-day. I am simply astonished that my hon. friend could be so right and at the same time so wholly wrong in such a short document. The minister is exceedingly right in some things he has done. He is exceedingly right, for example, when he gets rid of his receipt tax. His supporters too are exceedingly right when they refer to the taxes that have been got rid of as "nuisance taxes," taxes for which this government are responsible to the extent of one hundred per cent. In things like that the Finance Minister is absolutely right, but in many instances he is hopelessly wrong. I do not blame him, I do not think anyone ought to hold him up to censure, because at one time he had four portfolios to look after. I think the number he is administering now is three, and he has just had a chance at the budget when opportunity was given him, a chance snatched between runs from one department to the other. Then my hon. friend has other arduous duties to perform in keeping things straight around the Privy Council.
Just let us see how hopelessly wrong one can be sometimes. Let us take the income tax, for example. When my hon. friend introduced his budget he told us that all his proposals were in a downward direction. Times have been so good and the present government's administration has been so prudent, of course, that there is no suggestion of an advance in any direction. Every single step was toward a reduction. Then my hon. friend went on to say that he was making these reductions with a desire to make available new money for development. With this object in view he stated he proposed reductions all along the line. I pause at this stage to make this observation. If I had for one fMr. Gershaw.]
moment thought that the minister knew anything about these proposals I would have said that he was deliberatly deceiving the House and the country. But I do not make that charge. The department have drawn up these resolutions, they have prepared the new schedule. I do not know whether my hon. friend found time to read over his proposals or not, but I do know that he, like the rest of us, now knows that very large increases have been made in income taxes. There is no secret about it at all. We all know that a very large part of development, not only of this but of every country, is carried on through the activities of companies and corporations. Nevertheless my hon. friend doubles-well, you cannot say doubles exactly because all these things depend upon the incidence of the rate of taxation having regard to the assessment of an individual-but he practically doubles the taxes on the dividends of these companies. The Liberal policy here -I think it runs pretty fairly true to Liberal policies generally-is this: We want to secure new money for development, and in our endeavour -to secure new money for that purpose we propose to tax the capital so used at a higher rate than is imposed upon any other capital. We want to increase business, we want to increase development in the country, and so we are going to give those interested in development the opportunity of just paying double the taxes Which they would pay if they did not do anything to develop this Canada of ours. That is how this budget works out.
I ask my hon. friend this question:	What
is the capital in Canada that does the most useful w-ork? If my hon. friend answered fairly he would say "The capital which is supplying employment, the capital which is developing the country, the capital which is making the factory chimneys to smoke and the whole countryside to function." And my hon. friend would also say "There are two classes of capital. There is that class of capital which works for the country, and there is the capital that takes no chance whatever, the capital that exists in tax-free securities, the capital that is to be found in first-class mortgages, the capital that is to be found in bonds, the capital that is to be found in real estate and which depends entirely on the unearned increment from that real estate." There you have a different class of capital. No one who is either serious or honest will deny that the capital -which is desired, the capital which is of use to the country, is the capital which is engaged in the country's development and industrial work. The minister is applying a

The Budget- Sir Henry Drayton
double rate of taxation to useful capital but it is absolutely impossible to comprehend how, when applying the double rate of taxation, the minister can make the claim that it is being done for the purpose of aiding development. The thing is absolutely inexplicable unless the explanation is this:	That one
method of taxation may be temporarily popular and the other unpopular, and that all ordinary financial rules applicable to such a situation are to be swept to one side for the purpose of temporary political advantage. I am afraid the departmental officials did not fully instruct the Minister of Finance as to what they were doing.
My hon. friend claims there is a reduction in taxation of $25 000,000. Is there? We have not had any particulars at all as to how that reduction is made up. I am not going to ask my hon. friend for them now,
I do not suppose he has the data with him. He takes what the department has given him and, as I said before, he is running three departments; he has not had time to inform himself as to the details. But just let us see how this matter works out. Last year the companies were taxed to the amount of $31,091,274. That was the sum of money received from them, out of a total tax of $55,248,042. That means that we took out of these companies, whose dividends are now to be taxed twice, more than 55 per cent of all the money raised under our income taxation. We are told that there are no increases in this budget or in this taxation, while as a matter of fact we know that there are many cases where the rate of taxation is doubled as a result of these proposals. Setting aside the individual instances, let us consider the situation having regard to the statement made that the country is getting the benefit of the $25,000000 reduction. We took over $31,000,000 from these companies under a tax of 10 plus 5 per cent. That would make practically lOJ per cent and would mean that the earnings on which those taxes were levied approximated $300,000,000. Now I admit at once that all that money does not become subject to a double tax. It is only the amount of the company's earnings paid out in dividends that becomes subject to the double tax. All company earnings are now taxed under the budget 9 per cent instead of 10.5 per cent under the old law. Everything is taxed, but it is only the dividends that are subject to the double tax. It might be thought to have been entirely wrong. I am not now justifying it. It is true that I enforced it. It is true that I administered an act which is exactly the same, but it may well be asked, I admit, what is the fairness
of taxing companies on their total annual earnings, when a large amount of those total earnings have to be put back into the business for the purpose of carrying it on, and when the directors think that only a certain moiety, say 80 or 90 per cent, can safely be paid out in the form of dividends? I am not raising that point at all. That system continues. That is common, if it be an error, to my hon. friend, to myself and to our predecessors. But allowing for the difference between the $300,000,000 of earnings and actual dividends, I think my hon. friend will agree that $250,000,000 would be a fair amount to look upon as the dividend paying power of the companies and corporations in this country. I do not know whether my hon. friend has the information. If his department had not the information at the time they brought down this resolution and placed it in his hands, I should think they would have it now, so that they would know what they were doing, but I submit $250,000,000 would not be so very far out. Taking $250,000,000 as the dividend paying power of the companies in Canada, what are we assessing? I am aware at once, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians unfortunately do not own all those dividends or all that stock. In the year 1921 a return was brought down by the statistical department which showed that the amount of American holdings in the stock and bonds of our companies was considerably under a third. In 1920 a similar calculation was made by an American authority-my recollection is that the author was Mr. Fels
__where it was shown that Canadians owned,
. of their own investments, stocks and bonds in companies, over 64 per cent, the American holding being under a third, the balance being taken up by the British holdings and the holdings of other nationals. I am aware that in the last few years it has become a practice-well it is not a matter of declared government policy but it is a matter of the continued and continuous and everlasting handing over just a little bit more and a little bit more, a bit of Canada here and a bit of Canada there, this factory _here and that market there to the United Slates. That is the practice of this government, and the fact is that it has been the practice of this country, irrespective of any government, to a far greater extent than it had any right to be, but this government most markedly have never yet properly appreciated the necessity of a policy looking to the development of Canada for Canada, and by Canadians for Canadians. They have never yet got down to it, the trend has been much more marked and it is going on more and more all the time.
324S	COMMONS
The Budget

I am not prepared to say that the third of American holdings that I referred to is not now a half; it may be, but I hope it is not. I have not the recent figures but surely again it is not out of the way to assume that Canadians to-day hold 50 per cent of the stock and bonds in their own companies, and if that statement be correct, just see where the Minister of Finance finds himself placed in connection with his so called reductions. The reason why I am differentiating between Canadian and other holdings is that, as I understand it, it is only the Canadian investor who is subject to the double tax. If I am wrong the minister will correct me. Very well, I am cutting the dividends down then to $125,000,000 as against $250,000,000, and we have then under these proposals increased assessable wealth amounting to $125,000,000, to be assessed double for the first time by a government that actually claims its proposals are all reductions. The return to the government will depend entirely upon where the moiety and the average of the dividends will be assessable. If it is to be found in very large incomes, the increase in revenue will be enormous. If it be found on the other hand in the lower income the increase will not be as great.
My hon. friend will tell me at once if I am wrong in the figures which I take. This is only an estimate, a guess; it is impossible for anybody who is not in the office to do anything more than guess. But suppose we find this result that, out of the increase, this extra $125,000,000 of assessable wealth falls on the average within the class of incomes which, after all exemptions and allowances' for children, are taxable at $7,000, and we find that the average of the whole is to be represented by incomes of $7,000-in that case-and I do not think I am putting it at a very high figure-the rate would be seven per cent under my hon. friend's proposals. He will check me if I am wrong and I have not properly understood him although I think I have. The new revenue collectable would then amount under this budget that is supposed to be doing nothing but cutting taxation, to an extra tax collected from the people of $8,750,000.
Let us take another figure. If it be found that the average assessment in respect of that tax falls within incomes of the $10,000 class, the rate would be ten per cent and the extra taxation collectable from the people of the country would be $12,500,000. I do not know what information my hon. friend has as to where that average is to be found; but I know that if the average is where I suggest that will be the result, and I know that

irrespective of where it may be there is a very large increase in this item of income taxation directed by this government against an interest, a public necessity, namely, that of development which at the same time they are saying that these proposals are taken in ease of. I think my hon. friend will pardon me when I say that I look upon him with all amazement as being so absolutely right when he is referring to his nuisance taxes and the like, so absolutely wrong when he is referring to the effect of his proposals and the larger aspects of this case.
One question which I think deserves more than passing notice is raised by this budget: Have the people of this country, have those doing business in this country, the right to take the word of the government, the word of the Prime Minister as meaning anything? Of all the different ways in which pledges may be given by governments I would have thought that a Speech from the Throne would be one of the most positive, but I am not now referring only to that. We have the statements made by the leader of the government at Richmond Hill; we have the Kingston speech also made during the election campaign and many others. I am not referring to one thing by itself; but if there be anything which one would think ought to be observed it is the considered statement of the government, not made in the height of a political campaign, but contained in the Speech from the Throne. I bring this up not only because I think it is an absolutely vital matter, but because in bringing it up I desire at the same time to answer again statements which have been made by the leader of this government and other ill-advised supporters of it in connection with what occurred in 1921.
In 1921 there was a Speech from the Throne in which the statement was made that the tariff would be revised. The tariff was not revised, not because of any intervening action taken by the government, not because of any intervening question of political expediency which might affect the government, but simply and solely, as was stated at the time, because the United States government were considering whether they would make permanent or not tariff items which we rightly or wrongly thought to be very disadvantageous to this country and we were told from Washington that if we took that action which any self-respecting Canadian government would take on the assumption that those were to be permanent taxes, we might afford a further excuse for making these taxes permanent. I am going to refer to the reasons which were then given.
I do this because whenever this government have no defence-and it is very often they

The Budget- Sir Henry Drayton
have no defence; it is only an accident when they have one-their whole plea is that somebody else did it-the tu quoque argument.
A pledge was given by this government that there would be no interference in tariffs except on the report of the tariff commission. If that was not to be considered as a pledge, what was the reason for appointing the tariff commission? Was the only justification for the appointment of the tariff commission to give political friends salaries with empty offices and thus pile up expenses on the people? Or was the idea, as that pledge would indicate, that the tariff board was to function, and that no changes should be made before an investigation had taken place? This is not the only breach of faith on the part of the government which we have had to point out. This is not the only instance in which a promise has been given only to be broken. We have pointed out the same thing before, and always the answer is a shrug of the shoulders and " Oh, yes." And that is all. In 1921 there was a budget speech, from which I shall read. The tariff was going to be amended and it was not.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
says "hear, hear." This is his whole case. This miserable attempt has been made throughout the country ever since to make a case for disregard of promises out of the fact that the tariff was not altered at that time. Now I am going to ask the minister if he can fairly take exception to one single word that I shall now read. He cannot and I know he will not. I am reading now from the budget speech of 1921, dealing with this very question of the tariff.
The tariff deals with international business and the proper interests of the country can only be considered in the light of international business and the tariff laws of other countries.
Does my hon. friend object to that? Can anyone object to it? If so, we ought to find quarters for them in some other place.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Senate.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it will not be the Senate; we can find cheaper quarters for people of that sort.
It is idle to attempt to disguise the fact that any proper Canadian tariff must have consideration to the settled tariff conditions obtaining in the United States.
Does any hon. gentleman want to object to that? I think not.
Of our total trade of the past year 57 per cent was with the United States. Of total imports of $1,240,125,056, those from our neighbour to the south were $856,593,470 or 69 per cent of the whole. As already
pointed out, temporary tariff legislation of the United Staties would place a barrier against our exports to that country amounting to no less than $168,000,000. Such or similar action made permanent, of necessity, would require a careful and thorough revision of the Canadian tariff for the purpose of ensuring the proper continuance of Canadian business-of ensuring employment and Canadian stability-a matter of gravest moment to all classes of our citizens, of moment to the farmer as well as to the industrial worker, of moment to the farmer because of the home market-
Of course my hon. friends will not agree with that.
-always of importance and value to him, would become in view of the action of the United States and of the difficulties of financing overseas sales, more important than ever. . . . Under the circumstances, having special regard to the fact that there ought not to be a general revision of the Canadian tariff now and another after the close of the United States congress, no action will now be taken.
There is the reason no change was made at that time. And what did Mr. Fielding have to say on the question? At page 3154 of Hansard of 1921, he says:
I notice that the Minister of Finance made a very brief reference to the condition of the American tariff, though I must do him the justice to say that he treated it with more gravity than some people do. There are people throughout Canada who flippantly say that they do not care what the American tariff is.
Mr. Fielding did care, and so did I. And for that reason the government of that day was determined that in face of that temporary legislation which congress was considering making permanent, as un-5 p.m. fortunately has happened since, nothing would be done by this country which could for one minute afford the slightest excuse to any action that might be taken by the United States to our detriment. That is why no change was made in the tariff. It was not a question of the exigencies of Canadian politics nor was it a matter of making a concession for votes which otherwise we should not get. There was no suggestion of having to make appeals here and overtures there, for the fact of the matter is that we rather lost support. But what we did we believed to be the right thing and that is why we did it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did not Mr. Fielding conclude his observations on that day by moving an amendment?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is perfectly right; certainly he did. Throughout his speech he took the view that irrespective of the general conditions at that time it would be a good thing to get the Union government out of office, and he moved accordingly. How much real sincerity there was in the amendment my hon. friend will find if he consults the budget of 1922. Therein

The Budget

he will see exactly what Mr. Fielding thought at that time.
The shocking thing about the automobile reduction is that it seems to indicate on the part of the government a state of mind which evidently is above all ordinary considerations of honour or honesty. The government can say what it likes and promise what it likes and can change its mind just as it pleases. Furthermore, the tariff reduction in the case of automobiles exhibits the government's absolute disregard of consequences. I want the minister to correct me if I am wrong, but I have noticed in the public press advertisements showing that the tariff duty which the industry enjoyed before was not a net duty. Last session I took occasion to point out to hon. gentlemen, with much deference, that none of them knew anything about the tariff, for not one of them could tell me what the net protection was under any item contained in the schedule. We have had some light since. We have had Mr. Deachman's articles, which apparently constitute the only expert opinion the minister has received apart from certain references he has made to what the Chief Conservative whip and some others have said. But Mr. Deachman never pointed out what the net tariff was, and I notice the statement in the press that the net protection which the automobile dealers received before was 17 per cent. Did the minister inquire into that assertion and find it wrong? The net protection was 17 per cent as against an apparent protection of 35 per cent. Does my hon. friend quarrel with that? And what is the net protection which the minister is now giving with 20 per cent? Now, so far as the budget is concerned the net protection was never considered by the minister; I do not think I am unfair when I submit that it was never taken into account by the government. The item looked big and the manufacturers appeared prosperous, and there are a certain number of people who always like to throw a brick at anyone who they fancy is prosperous. The minister, I repeat, did not know what the net protection was, or at any rate he did not take it into account. If I am wrong he will contradict me. He does not contradict me, so that the government apparently has brought down these changes without knowing what the net protection was which the automobile industry was receiving, and without knowing what it was doing. They are learning now; they are getting the information, which should have been first obtained. It is quite possible, of course, for the government to do with the automobile

industry as they did with the farm implements business. It is quite possible for them to cut down the tariff on the one hand but by concessions, free materials, sales tax and the like not only to make up the cut, but even to exceed it. I do not know that the government intend doing that, but I want to point out that there has been a great change in industry since the war. I have in mind at the moment two factories operated in the same interest which, before the war, made carriage wheels. When the war started, in response to the demand for munitions these plants were converted into the making of shells. The war being over they were then converted into factories making automobile hubs and axles. They had to borrow money, something in the neighbourhood of 8450,000 if I remember rightly, in order to make that change. That firm is going to be wiped out as things now stand. Why should it be wiped out? Let us get some reasons. It paid $50,000 a month to Canadian workmen.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did it pay dividends?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Besides paying that amount it paid taxes to this government and to the municipalities, and for seven years paid no dividend whatever; last year a dividend of 5 per cent was declared. The minister did not know what he was doing; that is the real truth of the matter. He never deliberately set to work to injure such plants doing business, not in the manufacture of automobiles but in the making of parts. They were trying to develop this country; trying to give work to Canadians, trying to do just what the minister says he is trying to do in this budget, in reducing income taxes-make it more easy to get money for the development of Canada. But what he is doing is making sure that some of the money already obtained for our development will not be worth very much when he is finished with it. It is a serious thing if the people have not a right to accept the word of their government.
I know that great claims are being made by this government on the ground of the return of prosperity; I think my hon. friend calls this the " prosperity " budget. If he had really been seized of conditions and of what he was doing I think he would have called this the "gold brick" budget, instead.
Let us see where the prosperity is, and if we can find it. With those who have studied conditions I think it is common ground that following the war, deflation set in, reaching its culmination in 1921. During that time we went down and down, not only in Canada .

The Budget- Sir Henry Drayton
but practically throughout the whole world. The great United States had then not a few but hundreds of thousands, even millions of people out of employment; everyone felt it. That is surely common ground with both my hon. friend and myself. Does he deny it? I do not think he would. He certainly should not, and with his knowledge of the subject I am quite confident that he will not. Neither will he deny that that deflation was inescapable; it was forced on the country and was not the result of any governmental measure. We struck the bottom in 1921 and, in common with the rest of the world, began to pick up in 1922. There was progress everywhere; not very much in Canada, but a little.
In 1922 we had the first budget of the King government, in which were made irritating little changes here and there, although the budget did not really amount to anything one way or the other. The only bad thing was that it indicated a trend of policy dangerous to the country, dangerous to industry and to capital; it was an unsettling budget. There were no serious cuts; we used to call it the 2J per cent budget, but the underlying ideas and the statements made in the House were unsettling, as a result of which people thought it was not safe to go on and expand business. My hon. friend will also agree that that is not altogether a Conservative thought; that others than Conservatives knew that fact. The Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, in his budget speech of 1923, stated:
Business men do not' like to be always threatened with changes in the tariff.
He recognized then that business stability, which he desired, could not be obtained without tariff stability, and he further stated:
Speaking broadly, it is possible to give the country a reasonable assurance of stability of tariff. Such assurances are very desirable, for no business man would care to enter upon enterprises which may be brought into peril by frequent tariff changes.
Such statements are, of course, merely obvious truisms. Everyone knows them; everyone with any knowledge of business or financial affairs is fully aware of them. The country did not need to be told by the right hon. gentleman, but people were glad to get that assurance; the country quickly responded to this statement of policy, and conditions in 1923 improved.
Our return to normal conditions, Mr. Speaker, has always been held up from time to time; that has. been the trouble. We had a proper policy laid down, by Mr. Fielding in 1923 "tariff stability" and we had immediate action, with business starting to pick up again at once, with a greater volume of production. The
trouble is that we are always being halted and thrown back through this government forgetting all about pledges and statements. Under this government pledges were only made to be broken. We had a period of tranquillity and stabilization in 1923, but my hon. friend brought down his famous "death knell of protection" budget in 1924, and oh, what a year that was! Any member of the House who has followed things at all knows that 1924 was a very bad year. Conditions were better in 1923, but in 1924 the famous "death knell of protection" budget was introduced. Now this year the Minister of Finance says:
Nowhere are the results-
When pointing to the country's growing trade:
Nowhere are the results of this growing trade more accurately reflected than in the increased earnings of Canadian railways and in the annual statements of Canadian financial institutions and Canadian industrial corporations.
The minister is absolutely right in his reference to railway traffic. Railway traffic is an excellent barometer. The best barometer we have to-day, so far as this House is concerned, is found in the reports of our own ralway which have, been considered by committees of this House, and with which the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) is very familiar. He will be able to tell my hon. friend that he is entirely wrong from his knowledge of what the country did. He will be able to take the minister's barometer, the minister's yardstick, and say to the minister: Yes, there was nothing wrong done in 1925 as regards the tariff-some of the few still sane members of the Liberal party on fiscal questions saw to that-there was nothing wrong done as regards the tariff in 1925, and the country starts to pick up. We gained, certainly wre gained in 1925, just as wre gained in 1923, just as we go off in 1922, just as we come on after the pledge of the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding that there would be no more of this nonsense. We go down again in 1924 just so soon as notice is served on Canadian industry to get out, that the first step" has been taken. Then we have the reassuring budget of last year the effect of which was to increase the customs duties by approximately $1,000,000. Then when you get the country responding and going ahead again, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance this year tries to see if he cannot put another kink in that progress.
I said the hon. member for North Waterloo could show how wrong the minister is in thinking that the Canadian National figures

The Budget- Sir Henry Drayton
showed great progress. Let us see. This government always says that it has nothing to do with the management of the Canadian National Railways, and of course it has not, except sometimes when certain matters are up, perhaps a by-election here or a by-election there, and then they seem to get a little bit of assistance, which we do not think is quite right. But speaking generally they have nothing to do with the railway.

Let my hon.
friend just ask the minister next to him, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), and if his memory is good-sometimes it is bad-he will be able to tell him as to the political disclosures of certain reductions in rates in Nova Scotia which came very conveniently for a certain election.

speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend's memory is bad; I pass on.
There are two propositions here, Mr. Speaker. The first proposition is that the government has absolutely nothing to do with the railway net figures. The government can claim credit if, as a result of government fiscal policies, new industries are set going and there is increased production. It can claim credit for the gross revenue of the company, though most of the credit is the fields', I admit. If the traffic goes up markedly, the government can say: Look at this traffic; it shows the country is going ahead very well under our regime. The Canadian National figures dhow a drop in 1924 as against 1923 of 4,749,721 revenue tons. The yardstick of the railway's activities in freight, namely, the ton miles of revenue freight, fell off 1,613,998,426 revenue ton miles, and as a matter of fact there was a reduction in gross railway revenue that year of 117,547,305.
In 1925 the attack on Canadian industry ceased for the time being. With practically no tariff changes, the country starts to function better, and just here let me point out one peculiar thing which I commend to the study of the hon. member on the other side who has particular knowledge of the railway situation. This country really starts to get on its feet and get going when the government cannot function. If there is any moral to be drawn from last year it is that this government is of no help, but a danger to the country when it can function, but when it cannot function; when it is in dry dock wait-
ing for repairs; when 8.O.S. calls go out to the west and the embattled farmers are not here yet, and when the Governor General will not sign orders in council for them, the country starts to go ahead and do well. The moral is there; the facts also are there. Well, business improved in 1925. Does my hon. friend think business ought or ought not to improve having regard to the distance that Canada has travelled from the universal cataclysm of the war? Does he not think so? Does he not think our curve should be up? Does he not know it? If he thinks so, just let us see what he is doing when he refers to these railway figures. It is perfectly true that the railway figures my hon. friend has in mind show a net income of $32,264,414 in 1925 as against an income of $20,430,694 in 1923, but the hon. gentleman when he saw those figures forgot that the government had not anything to do with them, and that the whole betterment-did the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) say, Hear, hear?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. You are
stretching your imagination.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman just yawned. He is a good yawner.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not surprising either.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I admit that
some gentlemen would like to forget that the whole of that betterment is the result of economies in the administration of the railways and notwithstanding smaller revenues. The whole claim my hon. friend makes to improvement is to be found in those figures, and they are the only railway figures that will give him any comfort. I say there was less traffic, yes, less gross revenue and less traffic; for the Canadian 'National Railway statement shows that in 1925 the revenue was $244,971,202, while for 1923 it was $253,000,000 odd. What had this government been doing to the country in the meantime? Well, they had been playing with their tariff reductions. Instead of there having been progress from 1923 onwards there has been retrogression. Let us take my hon. friend's own yardstick, the business activities of the railways, and let us see what they disclose. They show a decrease in gross revenue of $8,164,285. It may be said that some of the orders made as to rates are responsible to some extent for that reduction. But that would not be true in the case of tonnage. In 1925, the great year of prosperity, according to my hon. friend, there was, as compared with 1923, a drop in revenue tonnage of 2,249,081 tons. There was also a drop of 519,614,436 ton miles of revenue

The Budget-Sir Henry Drayton
freight in that year of alleged wonderful prosperity. And the figures of our railway are confirmed by the government's own figures. The Dominion statistician has issued a report on railways, including of course the National railway, and that Shows a total freight of 103,75i,559 tons in 1923 as against 96,239,379 tons in 1925, a decrease in Canada's activities in 1925 as against 1923 of 7,518,180 tons. Perhaps I am wrong in using the expression "Canada's activities"-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Could not some of that reduction be attributed to the fact that the railways encountered motor truck competition?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ah! The motor truck is always with us. I did not notice that the minister said very much about that when he was dealing with the railways.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a fact though.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have to consider also the through traffic, but there is not much difference there; at any rate the difference seems to be fairly proportionate. I have not worked out the calculation myself, but looking at it roughly I do not think the difference would amount to a great deal. I have just taken the figures which the statistical department gave me as to the gross tonnage, and the hon. gentleman will agree with me that there is an astonishing falling off.
My hon. friend has been drawing certain conclusions from certain trade statistics. As to that he is right; the trade statistics standing by themselves are good. But taking his own figures as to the activities of our railways, and these trade figures, can they both be right? It is true that we are exporting much more than we formerly did, but do these figures alone indicate national prosperity? No, Canadian labour has not enjoyed its proper share of trade. The prosperity of the country, outside of certain lines, is unfortunately more fictitious than real. I put these questions to the Minister of Einance: Does he think that a country can really be said to be prosperous that has a diminishing home market? Does he not really think that it is a great thing to have Canadian labour employed and to have a large national payroll? I think he does. I think he would agree with me that no country can be said to be really prosperous whose home market is diminishing. The minister's own figures prove the truth of what I say. Taking his own yardstick as the gauge of prosperity, namely the business done by the railways, we find that we had less production 14011-207
in 1925 than we had in 1923. Can there be any doubt about that? The minister's budget speech, yardstick, shows it so there can be not much doubt about it. Our exports for the calendar year 1925-and I take the calendar year because our railways follow the calendar year-were 8254,569,672 greater than they were for 1923, and at the same time our imports for 1925 were less by 812,763,167 than they were for 1923. Smaller production, Mr. Speaker, with increased exports and lessened imports, indicate no general prosperity. Will my hon. friend claim that it does? Can anyone claim honestly that it does? Let me state it again. This is what the minister has proved:	There have been increased exports
and lessened imports. But smaller production, with increased exports and lessened imports, does not indicate general prosperity. What does it indicate? It indicates lessened domestic activities, a shrinking home market, a shrinking national pay roll-what else can it indicate? We might just as well be honest with ourselves-what else can it indicate? Here is the home production that much less. Here is that enormous increase in exports, and lessened imports. What does it amount to except that the great buying power of the country, which is always the wages of the masses, is not here to make its home purchases as it did in 1923?
Again, is this condition not another indication of what the exodus of our workers really means? I admit at once that certain price modifications will be found. In 1923 our wheat prices were not as good as they were in 1925. Therefore we got more dollars for tonnage exported in 1925 than in 1923. But that is only a modification; it does not furnish a complete answer. While we have had an increase in the case of wheat there have been declines in the case of other commodities. For example, we have had a drop in the price of paper-a very important article of commerce, as my hon. friend will admit. Does my hon. friend really think that exports, at the expense of a loss in the home market, make Canada prosperous? Does he not really know, as has been pointed out by an American authority, that Canada is borrowing? I am not now speaking of government borrowing. We never borrowed very much in New York, but eight months ago the direct government obligations of Canada, although three times as great as they were when this government took office, were small compared with the great borrowings which as a country we have made in New York. My recollection is that in 1915 or 1916, when the calculation was made, American investments



The Budget-Sir Henry Drayton
in Canada amounted to $420,000,000. I saw a statement, I think by the general manager of the Royal Bank-and it seems to be fortified by American authority-that the American investments in Canada to-day amount to approximately $2,500,000,000. Does my hon. friend not know that with the necessity for finding interest on that immense amount of money we must have larger exports? Here unfortunately we are not paying merely by these exports, increased as they are; but by the continued transfer of the natural resources of Canada to our friends to the south. Again, that a country cannot hold its own population is no indication of prosperity.
I am not going into figures which have been given before in regard to immigration. I will take the government's own figures relating to present conditions. The last I have been able to get are for January and February of this year. In January the number of immigrants entering Canada was 2,324, and in February, 4,396, a total of 6,720. As against the total immigration into Canada for the same two months in this wonderful year of prosperity, we find that the figures given by the Department of Labour of the United States show an emigration from Canada into the United States for January of 7,155 and for February 6,086, a total of 13,241 or 6,521 more than our total immigration for the two months-nearly double the number of people we have been able to get into this country, with all the millions we have been spending. My hon. friend will know very quickly when we have prosperity in this country: we will have it when we have work for the people who are here, thus obviating the necessity of their leaving. And you will have immigration to Canada when there is a job for the man who comes in. There will be immigration when money is really available for the development of the country, something which my hon. friend wishes, but which he takes such painful care in this budget to prevent.
I am now going to deal with the claim with regard to prudent administration. It is a lovely mouthful of words. I always like to take my hon. friend's own figures. He has been very good this year, in the preparation of his budget, in classifying the expenditures under different heads. He sets forth three different classes of payments which this country has to make-the principal expenditure attributable to the war, other fixed and public debt charges, and general expenditure. He then gives us the costs under those different headings which he conceives to be proper, and I am going to follow them as closely as I can.

I will first refer to the principal expenditure attributable to the war. I have taken my hon. friend's list and made out a similar list for 1921-22, dividing the expenditures as he has divided them. I have tried t-o make it so that it will be fair as a matter of comparison. For example, under the heading of National Defence is now grouped not only the militia activities but also the naval and air activities. I have put them all together, therefore, for 1921-22. In 1921-22 we collected our income tax through the Finance department; we now collect it through the Customs department, therefore I have transferred the item of the cost of collecting taxes from Finance in 1922 and put them under Customs, so that this item can be comparable. In connection with the first heading we have a reduction in cost. These war expenses in 1921-22 amounted to $179,264,098, and for the year just closed, $163,-
997,000,	a saving of $15,249,098. I wonder whether anyone who thought for a moment would not expect that? We have not had an intervening war. As we move from the war those costs go down. Take for example the drop between $9,000,000 and $10,000,000 under the head of soldiers' civil re-establishment. Does anyone claim credit on the part of the government for that saving? There simply was not another war. The number of men still to be taught by way of vocational training and otherwise is disappearing. There was no economy there; it was simply a case of less ground to cover. As a matter of fact, on fair grounds no credit whatever is to be taken by any government for the saving of that $15,249,089.
The next item is, other fixed and public debt charges. In 1922 those amounted to $27,034,553; for the past year they amounted to $31,458,000, an increase of some $4,400,000. Well that is an increase of this government, but it would be absolutely unfair to charge this government with the increase in discount and expenses of loans-just as unfair as it would be to charge the old government with the large item of premium, discount and exchange of $3,302,674 which was peculiar to 1922. Both are matters over which the administration as such had no control whatever. This administration has no control over the item which they have had to insert of $3,530,000 as against $82,636 in 1922 in connection with discount and expenses of loans. The accident is that the loans fell due and my hon. friend had to look after them. In 1922 the accident was that I had to produce a great deal of money for loans falling due in New York. My hon. friend nods his head in assent. I am giving

The Budget-Sir Henry Drayton
the government in this the benefit of $200,000 because their item is $200,000 more than mine
was.
Unless we throw both these items out I have an absolute right to take credit for making the country a great deal of money in connection with the item of exchange, because over and above every single penny paid out for premium, discount and exchange during those years of bad exchanges, we made $9,848,643. But I am saying nothing about that; it goes; it was an accident; it is something that does not enter into the details of ordin^ ary administration. I would do with that just as I would do with the other item which is against my hon. friend, namely, get rid of it. They ought both to be thrown out. The result there is that instead of an increase of $4,423,447, the real increase is only $976,083 I am not blaming my hon. friend at all in regard to it; he has added that in connection with not war pensions, but the pensions and superannuation of servants of the House. I am not saying anything about this addition of $976,0S3, but it is an addition.
I come now to general expenditures. For general expenditure the amount actually paid in 1921-22 was $159,421,140 as against $147,-
435,000	in 1925-26. If we deduct from that item of $3,292,674 that my hon. friend agrees should come out, just as I have taken off from his item of $3,447,364,-we have an actual decrease of $8,693,466. That means that this government had the right to say on these figures: We have run the business of the country for $8,693,466 less than in 1921-22. That falls very far short of the claims that have been made; but just let us look into what the figures of 1921-28 contain. I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me that it is not fair to charge the administration of 1922 with railway deficits which in his administration are transferred to the railways. No man with any ordinary sense of fairness would suggest that. Yet we were charged in 1922 with railway deficits amounting to $6,386,800 for running expenses and $1,364,254 for capital.
We used to help the provinces under the Agricultural Instruction Act. My hon. friend wipes that out. The government say that while they admit agricultural instruction to be a good thing, it is immoral to help the provinces with money raised by Dominion taxation. I might point out in passing how briefly this government can stay with anything, because only this very year we have this proposition that so long as the provinces want money wrung from the Dominion taxpayer, not for the laudable purpose of agricultural instruction but for the equally laud-14011- 207J
able purpose of old age pensions, it is quite moral and proper to give it to them. So it is. As the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) suggests, one means votes in this House and the other does not.
Under the Highways Act payments to the provinces are reduced by $1,399,008. There is no administration there, under the terms of the act the payments are reduced. I wonder if the government think we should also compare this item of $5,592,703, the final payment for the government's shipbuilding programme which was stopped in 1928. Are they entitled to any great credit because they have not gone on with another? Nevertheless, for the purpose of comparison that is what they must urge, although it is ridiculous to attempt such a comparison. All these items together make a total of $15,769,335. We have the reduction of $8,693,466 shown by including all these items which are not the subject of comparison under the wildest guess, because the work is all stopped or transferred to the provinces or the railways. The government cannot throw the money away for these purposes even if they want to do so; there is no demand on them for it. In order to find the correct result, therefore, we must deduct from those non-comparable items of $15,769,335 the alleged saving. What do we find? In this past year when things are supposed to be more nearly normal, when difficulties are supposed to be composed, we find that the government have actually spent in comparable sendees $7,075,869 more than was spent by the government in 1928.
In getting at that result I am not taking the figures down to the last five cent piece or anything like that; I am taking them by and large. For example in 1928 we had all the cost of the Grand Trunk arbitration which amounted to something like half a million. I am not taking that off, although there was nothing last year to compare with it. I recognize that from time to time you have these different items; you have something one year and something else another year. It is therefore not fair to strike them off, but it is absolutely unfair to seek to compare accounts with other accounts which contain items and liabilities entirely transferred on to other shoulders, items transferred to the provinces and items transferred to the railways.
So that this " prudent administration " just comes down to this, that in respect of comparable items and expenditure within their control the government have managed to spend in the last year of grace $7,075,869 more than the former government, whom they accuse of such frightful extravagance, spent
