speechtext:
The Budget-Sir Henry Drayton
I say we did not do it. On the other hand, as far back as 1919-20 we recognized the fact that the railways stood on our books for far more than they were worth, and we treated $284,000,000 odd in that one year as inactive, something which could not be relied upon, something which certainly was bringing in no income, and we increased our net debt accordingly. Some hon. gentlemen who were not in the former House may not be quite familiar with this. We arrive at our net debt by deducting from our gross debt our assets, and when we ourselves knew that we had not the assets there, we thought we might just as well be honest to the country and to outsiders and say so, and so we did. We took off that sum, which had the effect of adding to our national debt in that one year $284,000,000.

In 1920, and
that has been referred to by supporters of
the government. I will not say that any members of the government were quite so foolish as to do it, but the increase in the debt that year has been referred to as an evidence of improper Conservative administration when the whole fact of the matter is that it was simply a belated statement of truth. That is what we did.
Now I am going to put on Hansard the figures taken from the books of the Finance department and from the public accounts showing exactly how this debt question has been treated. In the first instance, the statement shows the net national debt at the end of each fiscal year ending March 31st; these are the figures of the Minister of Finance and of his department. No such charge can be made for 1920 when we voluntarily added $284,000,000 to the debt, nor in 1921 when debt retirements were actually $6,382,626 more than the guarantees.
Then the year 1922 comes along, and in that year the endorsements amounted to $61,000,000; the retirements amounted to only $48,871,443. Now of that year this administration was responsible only for the final quarter. I think, as a matter of fact, the railway payments had been made in the first part of the year; I do not think railway guarantees were given during the latter part of the year. I may be wrong in that, but it makes no difference. Right or wrong, there was only one government re-

figures, and that was this government. These figures are marshalled in March, of 1922; the Conservative administration went out of power in December, of 1921. But the whole defence is that we did it. Well, as a matter of fact, we had absolutely nothing to do with the marshalling of these figures. Payments are made from time to time in the Finance department, the same as in any other department, from cash on hand as the necessity arises, but the marshalling is always done, as it ought to be done, in the department itself, when the accounts for the year are being made up. So the result of it is for those three years, that we have a surplus, the last year, of guarantees over debts paid of $12,000,000 odd, and taking the full three years into consideration we have a surplus of $5,745,931 of guarantees over the debts paid off.

The Budget-Sir Henry Drayton
In the year 1923 we have a large sum of money coming in from England, something not earned by this government at all, something earned by the transactions of the former government with the Mother Country. That money is paid in cash. The government has the cash and they pay the whole of the commitments thrown upon them in cash, namely S77,863,936. The next year, 1924, simply because this government has not the cash, we start in with heavy guaranteees, and guarantees were given amounting to S72,500,000, as against retirements of $11,469,369; and in 1925, $81,000,000 as against retirements of $24,007,533.
Everyone agrees, first, 'that the property is not worth anything like what we have against it; secondly, that all the cash payments 'through all these years have been treated as money put away, treated as money bringing in nothing, treated as a dead asset, and they have not been deducted from the gross debt. Hon. ' gentlemen will also see that the real controversy turns entirely upon these two years, 1924 and 1925, where we have a net addition of guarantees over and above debts-and therefore of liabilities 100 per cent-of $118,000,000.
In the first instance, Mr. Speaker, let us just consider the absurdity of this position. When the money is your own money that you can afford to put into the property it is gone. It is no good, it is something to be written off. When you have no money and you borrow and get the cash, as was the case in some of the previous years, again the money that you borrow and put in yourself is gone. It is not deducted from the gross debt. On the other hand by some peculiar kind of-well it is not reasoning, it is misleading the public-

speechtext: Juggling.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, "juggling"
is a better word. Where you do not get money out of your own pocket, or on your own bond, but simply endorse the bonds of your agent who cannot pay you-namely the board -in that case the investment is perfectly good, and there is no responsibility. The thing is so perfectly ridiculous that my hon. friends were very well advised in the past when they admitted that there was no defence of the practice except the defence of "you did it." Now, I will simply put on Hansard the figures. The addition which ought to have been made to the net debt of the country for these years is $118,023,098. That is made up in this way: In 1924 the bonds guaranteed amounted to $72,500,000 odd, less redemptions of $11,469,369, leaving of increased responsibility $61,-
030,631. In 1925 the bonds guaranteed amounted to $81,000,000, less redemptions of $24,007,533 odd, leaving $56,992,467 added to the country's liability. Total $118,023,098.
I am not going to say anything about the little differences we have had in connection with fixing our national debt. We have had a revaluation of securities in the past, for example in connection with the debts contracted by Roumania and Greece, and the course followed by the directors of the late lamented Home Bank, which added pretty well to the showing for the financial year in which the particular arrangement was adopted. Now we had a change of ownership in connection with an elevator at Vancouver, built, if I am correct, by the Conservative administration. A debt reduction follows in the case of this elevator because it has 'been transferred to the commissioners at Vancouver and they are paying interest. In that case technically I think they are right because any investment which is paying interest ought, I think, to be deducted.
With these aids the Minister of Finance now calculates our net debt as $2,395,084,685. But if we are to be fair to ourselves and to the country we have got to add the $118,023,098, the increase of the country's railway guarantees over obligations retired, which makes the net debt not $2,395,084,685, as the minister states -but $2,513,107,783, or $90,971,982 more than when the present government took office. Whatever defence may be hunted up by the government I hope it is not going to be the same defence as in the past, namely, "you did it." I have given the actual figures, and they cannot be controverted by the minister. Why, I am fairer to the minister than he is to himself. Take for example his statement as to guarantees. Last year over and above retirements he says it was $64,000,000. In my calculation I did not bring it as high as that, I Only made it approximately $56,000,000.

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

We have not had the truth in the past, but we ought to have it in the future so that there should be no dispute about the matter. The figures of the department have been given. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have shown what the figures for the national debt really are. I have also demonstrated what the results have been of the so-called "prudent administration." speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a short time
will suffice for me to say what I have to say with regard to the budget.
First of all, let me call the attention of the House to one or two items in the estimated expenditure which I think are of vital interest. The Minister of Finance has given the expenditures attributable to the war as $163,997,000 or 47.83 per cent. Subsequently he shows that these are not all the expenditures, and he enumerates a number of other items which I take it would bring the total lip to over 50 per cent. It ought to be clearly understood by the people that of the total annual expenditures which we make here, fully one-half goes toward the payment of the interest charges of the last war. We are told that we need some war memorials. I would suggest that in this huge amount we have a very imposing war memorial, and one that is likely to prove very enduring indeed. Notwithstanding that huge amount, I observe that later on the amount proposed this year for what is called " national defence " is higher than the entire amount proposed to be spent on civil government. I know some hon. members in this House are inclined to take some of us to task because we take the opportunity from time to time of calling the attention of the government and of the country to the necessity of reduction in our war expenditures and the futility of war expenditures. Sometimes the papers take a fling at us and say we are making our annual speech on the war proposition, but I cannot accept this budget without emphasizing these figures given to us very clearly by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that show that we spend half our entire income upon war expenditures connected 
with the past war. As long as that situation continues it seems to me we are fully justified in discussing any measures that would tend to prevent any future occurrence of this kind.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What part
of that expenditure would the hon. member eliminate, or what part could be eliminated?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will come to that a little later. It is there now as a charge, but I suggest here merely that we should be very careful not to do anything that might increase the charge in the days to come.
There are other fixed and public debt charges amounting to 9.17 per cent of the total expenditure on government services. That means that fully 60 per cent of the entire expenditure of this country is what is termed fixed charges, so that at the best we in this House have control over less than 40 per cent of the expenditures. Again, of that 40 per cent a very considerable proportion of that amount is in the form of certain statutory expenditures; so that after all the amount that we directly control in this House is comparatively small.
I do not intend to enumerate the items which were given us by the Minister of Finance, but I might note two or three by way of illustration. For example, for the health of the people of this country we spend .19 per cent of our total expenditure. For scientific institutions we spent .29 per cent. For labour, a department in which I am of course interested, I note we spend .36 per cent. These most important departments of our public life are of such insignificance in the eyes of the parliament of this country that adding these three items we spend less than one per cent in carrying on what some of us regard as very important matters. We have, however, the opportunity of making some savings, it seems to me, even within the limits which I have indicated. We all recognize that in the co-ordination of the civil service we might effect very considerable saving. I should like to read a sentence or two from the Ottawa Citizen of January 26, 1926, which indicate the possible extent of such saving. On the editorial page there are certain facts and considerations as follows:
1. That the National Civil Service Reform League of the United States estimates a loss of $750,000,000 per annum in all government services or 25 per cent of the whole.

The Budget-Mr. Woods-worth
2.	That in Canada there is an approximate comparative loss of $60,000,000 through loose, inefficient, and non-competitive government business.
3.	That in 1918 the total personnel in the federal civil service was taken out of patronage and placed under open competition, or merit. To-day 33i per cent of these positions have been returned to the patronage system as political plunder.
I think that any one who wishes well for the future of Canada will come to the conclusion that we must not return any further along the road of patronage. I do not intend to discuss to-night the weaknesses that have been exhibited in our civil service. We are all aware of these from the recent investigation, but at the same time, as a country we cannot afford to return to the patronage system. We should restore to an independent commission those positions which have been taken back under government patronage. The same -might be said in regard to the great purchasing agencies where undoubtedly a large amount that is now expended, might be saved. Such a procedure would also greatly improve the general morale of the public.
Turning for a few minutes to the revenue side of our account, I note that from the income tax we received only 14.73 per cent of our total ordinary revenue. We have had a great deal of discussion in the last three weeks in this House in regard to the reduction in the income tax. It would seem to me that we have not so fully borne in mind that, after all, the income tax forms a very very small proportion of the total taxation of the people of this country, being less than 15 per cent. There are those who have objected to the income tax on the ground that we need more money for our investments. I am inclined to think that those who make such statements have not given sufficient attention to the underlying economic conditions. Our banks say they have money standing idle at the present time. I should like to suggest that instead of more money for investments we need greater buying power on behalf of the great masses of the people of this country. I would commend the Minister of Finance for reducing the taxes on the low incomes, and I would commend him for distinguishing between the incomes derived from earnings and the incomes derived from investments, but I am sorry to see any lessening of the tax on the higher incomes. On the other hand, I should like to see these very greatly increased, because as it is we are giving larger and larger amounts for investments, perpetuating and accentuating one
of the evils from'which the people are suffering the world over.
Certain hon. gentlemen have been ridiculing the analysis of the economic situation which was made a few years ago before the Banking and Commerce committee. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) and the Minister of Finance himself have laughed at the analysis which was made there. There are many thoughtful students of economics today who are voicing some of those opinions in ever louder tones. I should like some hon. gentlemen if they have time to read this article which I note in the April number of the Atlantic Monthly, because it contains in summary form an argument which has been recently set forth in a very important book on Profits, by Foster and Catchings. I want to read just a paragraph or two that will give the idea of the argument. For example the article states:
The engineering societies, under the direction of Herbert Hoover, have shown that we are already equipped to double our volume of production.
That is, instead of wanting to invest more fixed capital in railways, factories and other machinery of production, we have already at the present time capacity on this continent more than to double our present production. Why then do we want more investment? The trouble fundamentally is, as the article goes on to show:
What the people must have if prosperity is to last is the money with which to pay for goods rather than more and more devices for enabling them to acquire goods for which they do not pay.
We are told and we have been told in thi3 House that the labouring people are receiving higher and yet higher wages. The authors of this article go on to say:
The recent researches of Paul H. Douglas, soon to be published, show that the gain in real wages in the United States from 1890 to 1919 did not average one-half of one per cent a year. For a generation or two we have fallen far short of making the gains in human welfare which should have resulted from our scientific progress.
Progress towards greater total production and resultant higher standards of living is retarded because consumer buying does not keep pace with production.
In rather a humorous way the authors of this article, which is entitled "The Dilemma of Thrift," put the situation which faces us at the present time.
What a mess we get into! We work hard to pile our shelves high with what we most desire, and then we have to stop working because we are unable to take these things off the shelves and enjoy them. Though we produce much less than we could easily produce, we do not distribute to advantage even what we succeed in producing. We condemn extravagant buying at the very time when industry slows down because people are not buying enough. Then, while business wanes because it lacks consumers, we put taxes on

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
consumption; and, precisely \^ien 'business is in greatest need of people with incomes to spend, we reduce those incomes by reducing wages and dividends. We celebrate "buyers' week" and "thrift week" at one and the same time. By investing our savings, instead of spending them, we deny ourself to-day in order to produce more in the future, although we are already equipped to produce more than we know how to use. While many at home are in want, we strive more and more to send more of our wealth abroad; but we are loath to import much in return. Nations, at least, seem convinced that it is more blessed to give than to receive. A topsy turvy world! Alice in Wonderland found nothing more paradoxical.
I would like to turn back to our accounts for a moment. I said that we received only 14.3 per cent from our income tax, but we expect to receive from our excise taxes, namely sales tax, stamp tax and so on, 25.35 per cent, and from our customs import duties 33.80 per cent. It is not the income taxes that weigh the heaviest or that weigh at all upon the ordinary citizen. The great majority of Gur wage-earners and the lower salaried men in this country do not pay income tax at all. The tax that weighs on the ordinary citizen is the indirect tax such as the sales tax and the import tax and on this customs import duty alone we pay 33.80 per cent. The greater part of our taxation comes ia this indirect way.
In our income taxation we have been very careful to exempt those who have children; the more children you have, the less heavy the income tax weighs. But in the case of indirect taxation the more children you have, the heavier the tax, because of course we have heavier expenditure for food, clothing, housing and all along the line. So that in these indirect taxes which form the great bulk of the taxation which is placed upon the people of this country, there is not only no exemption for those who have the heaviest burdens to carry, but an added tax on those who are already overburdened. That is about the situation as we find it with regard to our estimated expenditure.
I have spoken of the way in which we may conserve something of the comparatively small amount of our revenues over which we have control. Just to illustrate some questions which arise outside of this parliament building but which receive scant attention inside, I should like to quote a paragraph from an address recently delivered by Dr. C. D. Howe, Dean of the Faculty of Forestry of Toronto University, to the Canadian Club According to the Ottawa Citizen, he said:
In the last seventy-five years nearly a million square miles of forests have been destroyed by fire in Canada. Even to-day three million acres are burned each year, equivalent to a strip of land a mile wide from Halifax to Vancouver. Does it matter who is Prime Minister as long as we continue to lay waste our forest wealth at the rate of three million acres a year?

This is my point: We spend a great deal of time talking about a few dollars rise or fall in income tax, about a few cents rise or fall in certain customs duties, while in the meantime great economic questions find hardly any place in the discussions 'which go on in this House. I think Mr. Howe is quite right in the question which he asks:
Does it matter who is Prime Minister as long as we continue to lay waste our forest wealth at the rate of three million acres a year?
I will not take the time of the House to go into the way in which we have been dissipating many of our other natural resources. There came into- my hand only a few weeks ago a paper delivered last March by Mr. C. M. Campbell before the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, on our Canadian natural resources. Some of us have been rather prone to emphasize the fact that we have almost unbounded natural resources in this country, but these scientists are now beginning to tell us that we have been altogether to optimistic with regard to these matters and that already our soils are being depleted, our forests are rapidly diminishing and even our mines are not nearly so extensive as we have imagined them to be. These things, it seems to me, should give us pause, and instead of spending three or four weeks in discussing what, after all, are almost entirely political matters, we as representatives . of the people ought to spend a great deal more of our time in considering the conservation and the proper utilization of these great natural resources.
I wish hon. gentlemen could read a little book, The Tragedy of Waste, by Stuart Chase, with regard to the wastes that are occurring on this continent through lack of co-ordination in the management of our industrial affairs. I remember several years ago reading an interesting little book by King C. Gillette, a practical business man who was accustomed to sizing up industries from the standpoint of the efficiency engineer. He looked over the industrial field and asked whether we were at all efficient? He said, among other things:
The engineers estimate that the loss to industries, through lack of efficiency is as follows: Mens' clothing industry, 63.78 per cent; building industry, 53 per cent; printing industry, 57.61 per cent; boot and shoe industry, 40.93 per cent; metal industry, 28.66 per cent; textile industry, 49.20 per cent.
This, he points out must average something like 50 per cent, a loss which he thinks is chargeable to lack of co-ordination. In the author's opinion, an individual under the system of co-ordination which he is advocating could produce enough in five years to

The Budget-Mr. If ood-sworth
maintain him for a lifetime of seventy years, no matter how extravagant he might be. This comes, not from some university professor or from some academic dreamer, but from a practical business man who, after looking over the arrangements of our industrial system as it operates to-day, suggests that there are great gaps to be filled in and duplications to be cut out, and that co-ordination is absolutely necessary if we are to produce and distribute economically and avoid the waste which is now taking place. I suggest that if our industry is 50 per cent inefficient we should pay a little more attention to recommendations of that kind and less attention to protecting our industrial concerns from outside competition. Let me say again, as I have said before that in my judgment neither protection nor free trade will solve our present problems; we must get behind all that and recognize clearly that solutions which perhaps might have been satisfactory some years ago are no longer feasible inasmuch as new factors have entered the industrial field in recent years.
There is one other matter to which I desire to call the attention of the House in connection with our financial statement. I have spoken of the estimated expenditure and the estimated revenue and made a few comments in each case. There is also the balance sheet, if I may so describe it, which the minister ha3 submitted to parliament. On March 31, 1925, our net public debt stood at $2,417,437,685.59, and the minister estimates that there will be a decrease in the debt this year to the extent of $22,353,000 odd. That sounds a large amount, and as some hon. members of the opposition have pointed out it is only apparent in view of the fact that the Canadian National Railways have not been taken into account. Personally I hope the time is not far distant when, in preparing the balance sheet, our government will include the Canadian National Railways among the public works of the country. But after all, it must be remembered, this apparently large decrease of $22,000,000 which is anticipated is less than one per cent of the debt, so that if the Canadian National Railways are taken into com sideration it is evident that we are not even paying the interest on our debt, let alone reducing the debt. That is the great point for us to emphasize. Most of us are unable to think in terms of millions or billions, but there are few who are incapable of thinking in percentages, and that is why I am trying to emphasize the percentages. We are therefore reducing the debt nominally by less than one per cent. And while this is an improvement on previous years it is still a very small reduction and does not touch the main problem at all.
As I have pointed out before, it is somewhat difficult for those of us who
9 p.m. belong to the minor parties to know how to vote on the budget, for the simple reason that only one amendment is permissible. We have therefore to vote for or against the amendment, and then for or against the main motion, for under normal circumstances we have no means, of stating what we think should be the fiscal policy of the country. It may be, in fact it is true, that we in the labour movement are so small numerically that it could make no immediate difference to the House or to the country what we might propose as a fiscal policy. Nevertheless we are here to submit our policy to parliament, and as I cannot move an amendment to the budget I want to put on Hansard again, as I did two years ago when I had an opportunity of proposing an amendment to the budget, the views of those whom we labour members represent in this House.
With regard to taxation we believe (a) in the abolition of fiscal legislation that fosters and sustains class privilege; (b) in the removal of taxes from the necessities of life; (c) in the taxation of land values; and (d) after the exemption of small incomes, in a steeply graded income and inheritance taxation. And the eleventh plank of our platform provides for a capital levy for the extinction of the war debt.
I want to call the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to the last two proposals. I cannot see why we in this country ought not as a federal government to impose an inheritance tax.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member add that tax to the inheritance tax already imposed by the provinces?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. Some of the provinces have an income tax which their citizens have to pay in addition to the federal income tax and I see no reason why we should not have a federal inheritance tax. In this connection I would observe that as between administrative bodies taxation is after all merely a matter of adjustment, and it is one that could be worked out between the Dominion and the provinces. I am inclined to think that in some respects the federal government have pre-empted too great a proportion of the taxation of the country. However, I am not discussing that question at the moment; rather, I am considering the principles underlying the proposal for an inheritance tax. I believe that we are absolutely right in suggesting that after a certain exemption, sufficiently large
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

to enable a man's estate to provide for his immediate dependents, the rest of that estate ought to be very heavily taxed. Personally I would go a great deal further: I would say that it ought to be expropriated.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What would be the limit?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not make any sugestion offhand; I am merely stating a general principle. But I would allow au exemption sufficiently large to enable the estate to take care of the man's immediate dependents, to give them a start in life, and after that I should think the state might very well take over the remainder. After ali, when you come to financial wealth you must remember that you are dealing with something that is different from the real wealth of the country. In the case of real wealth the more I have the better it is for me and it is none the worse for you, but in the case of financial wealth, dollars and pounds, the more I have the worse it is for the community, because after all the dollar is simply an order on the services of the rest of the community. If we allow large numbers of these orders to be passed on from generation to generation it means that the rest of the community, that the unborn children of the rest of the community, are saddled with debt and have to pay services for which those who inherit these orders have rendered no real value. These are considerations to which we should give attention.
I would go further than this. With regard to the war debt, as has been suggested in a good many countries, we should go beyond taxing the income and tax the principle. In previous years I have called the attention of the House to what I think should be very clearly recognized by all Canadians. During the war we paid very little of the war expenditure; we simply borrowed and borrowed and put off until after the war the settling of accounts. The result was that a large number of people were enabled to profiteer during the war. Since the war we have issued a large number of tax-free bonds, and a large number of people indirectly profited by the war after it was over. And what is the result? The greater part of Canada's debt is not owed to people outside of this country; if it were it might then be regarded as an international debt which we were under obligation to pay. - But the greater part of that debt is owed to people within the bounds of Canada, which simply means that we are drawing in these large revenues from different sections of the country, from the mass oi
	.
the Canadian people, and turning them over to another group of Canadians, who I fancy do not constitute a very large group. Over a hundred million dollars a year is being drawn from the mass of Canadians to pay those comparatively few who own our war debt, and over half this amount is in tax free bonds. It often seems to me that we in this House are not occupying a very enviable or exalted position, when our job seems to be that of a great collector, drawing from every man from Halifax to Vancouver what little sums he can afford; securing these not from him directly but indirectly through the things he buys; collecting all these little driblets from the different sections in order that, when we have collected them, they may be turned over to the few people who really control the situation. I do not know whether the bankers' proposition which is now put forward by the International Bankers would be a very great departure from the present scheme of things. They propose to collect the debts directly instead of through the different governments. I am not sure whether or not that would be feasible. After all the end is the same, whether debts are collected through the governments or directly; it means that a certain group of Canadians are paying tribute to another group of Canadians, and in regard to the returned men I would say that they are paying with the rest of the citizens, and paying heavily, in these forms of taxation, especially in the indirect taxation which forms so large a part of what we are able to collect.
I had not intended to say very much with regard to this budget as it affects labour. I think we may say that on the whole it is a fairly satisfactory middle class budget. So far as it may stimulate general prosperity, and lessen unemployment it may be beneficial to the workers. But on the whole it does not relieve to any great extent the burden which the workers are now carrying.
Since a good many gentlemen have brought up the matter during this debate, I would frankly admit that a good many of the labour men in eastern Canada are protectionists, and that they vote Conservative. That is their right, but I would also suggest that a very large number of these same people are not at all in favour of political action on the part of labour. Some of us in this country are trying to develop along the British lines, rather than along American lines. One of the Toronto members referred in eulogistic terms to Mr. Samuel Gompers, and thought we should follow his lead and not draw labour into the political sphere at all. I would like to say that some of us who have had British

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
training do not propose to take the lead in political matters from Mr. Samuel Gompers or those who have accepted his policy. We are following, and propose to follow much more closely, the example of the British Labour party.
An appeal was made the other day in front of this building by a large delegation from' one of the industrial centres of the western part of this province, and we were told that theirs was the voice of labour. I mingled with that throng and talked with a good many of the men. I was very much interested in discovering that they were very carefully marshalled by their employers. I was rathe: surprised to learn that they had even brought the company's police along, in order to keep order among themselves. I would also like to call attention to the fact that within those factories represented in that delegation there is no labour organization, so those people who are not yet strong enough to organize in their own behalf were the people brought down here by their employers to present their case. I do not at all question that they believed theirs was almost a holy crusade; I know that was their belief, but I would like to say thai these men had given very little attention to the underlying factors in their problems.
Labour after all is only one factor in the cost of production, and wages bear very little relation to the service rendered by labour. Before sitting down I should like to repeat some figures given in a previous debate by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). He pointed out that protection amounted to 35 per cent, but that the wages and salaries amounted to only 16J per cent; that is, the protection afforded was more than double the wages and salaries. He went on to say:
For 1924 the total salaries and wages paid by the automobile industry was $14,219,137 and the value of their production $88,000,000. Wages and salaries were therefore 16.1 per cent of the value of the production. The protection enjoyed is 35 per cent, and the increase in price over the United States price is also 35 per cent. In other words, the increased price which our automobile manufacturers exact from the Canadian people because of the tariff is twice the total salaries and wages paid by the industry.
Supplementing those remarks I would give these figures. The Ford Company book for 1925 shows salaries and wages of $10,13S,927; the Financial Post of February 12, 1926, shows the net profits of that company for 1925 as $6,131,352. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that these figures amply bear out the statement I made a few moments ago, that labour is only one-and in this case a minor-factor in the cost of production, and further that the wages paid seem to bear very little relation to the service rendered.
The budget from our standpoint is by no means what we would like to have it. As far as the people whom we specially represent are concerned, it does not relieve their burdens a very great deal, and yet I believe that there are certain important reductions which will be beneficial to the country as a whole, and therefore, as we cannot propose our own policy in an amendment, we intend to vote for the budget.
May I add a few general considerations. I believe that to-day we of the Labour group are representing not merely so many hundreds or so many thousands of a particular class, but are representing a new principle in the political life of this country, and that is the principle that we should elevate human rights above property rights. In the past, the polices of the older parties have on the whole been so dominated by what we commonly call the big interests that the ordinary men and the ordinary women across this country have had comparatively little chance. I do not wish to precipitate any general discussion, but I should like to make a reference to the Old Country where things are taking place to-day that are profoundly influencing the thought of the people not only all over Great Britain but in Canada as well. I have no desire whatever to-night to discuss the merits of the great industrial strike that is taking place in Britain, but I would like to take advantage of the attention that is being focussed on that great strike and which is forcing us to think, to consider for a moment some general conditions that exist in this country as well as in Great Britain. One of our local papers, the Ottawa Journal, in its issue of May 7th, said in an editorial headed "Let Canada Keep out of It," dealing with this industrial strike:
Labour and Farmer organizations in Canada might well refrain from interfering with the strike in Great Britain. The strike is a purely British matter, and a very vital one.
A good rule to follow in such leases is to try to let the people in their own country work out their own destiny in their own way.
I want to congratulate the Ottawa Journal on taking that stand. I think it is veiy interesting to find that the Journal has put it in that way. I hesitated a great deal to mention this matter until I Saw that some Conservative organizations had begun to communicate with Mr. Baldwin in connection with his policies, and I find , that certain of our own journals would like to dictate to our citizens as to what action they should privately take on a matter of this kind. It is all very well to let the people in the Old Country settle their own matters in their own way. I tried
326G
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

to say that in a discussion on imperial relations the other day and I found that there were hon. gentlemen who told me that that was going to disrupt the empire, that we as a Dominion ought to be interested in all that concerned the welfare of the empire. Let the British government settle the industrial dispute by all means, but I would like to ask very frankly: how about the case when some opium dealers want to force the opium trade upon China? How about the case when some diamond capitalists want to force certain policies in South Africa? How about the case when certain cotton growers want to retain certain very important privileges in Egypt? How about the case when certain big oil companies want to get concessions in the Near East? How about the case a few years ago when certain concessionaires wanted to get control in Siberia, when we interfered to the extent of an expenditure of several million dollars? I say that if we propose to apply this rule with regard to one part of the policy of the British Empire, it is well that wo should remember that we should apply it with regard to all the policies of the empire. An editorial the next day stated:
It is, we think, a profound error to regard the present general strike as an ordinary industrial conflict. It is something mudh more serious.
Agreed, but what is it? Briefly, the coal industry as at present organized cannot provide at the same time profits for its owners and a living wage for the miners. I think that is conceded in almost every editorial that we have had given to us. The owners, on the one side, refuse to reorganize and, on the other hand, they refuse to relinquish their profits. The miners, on their side, refuse to lower their standards of living and demand reorganization of the industry. I refer to this matter simply because the situation in the Old Country puts before us in a dramatic form the struggle that we have the world over and the fundamental cleavage that divides us here in this country when we come to a consideration of our financial affairs.
An hon. gentleman asked me a few moments ago-he is no longer in his seat-how would we deal with the debt? It is taken for granted that the debt is something that is inviolable, even though it has to be paid to Canadians. It is regarded as something we must not touch, that interest upon it is the first charge. It is that position, Mr. Speaker, that I want to take this opportunity to challenge. We say that the rights and the needs of the ordinary people of this country is a first charge on industry, and if there is a con-
[Mr. WoodsworthJ
flict between these two, we say that the needs of the men and the women and the children must come first, and I would like to see that general principle translated into our budget statements in the years to come.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member would favour repudiating the payment of interest on the public debt?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I said this-I do
not know whether the hon. gentleman was here a few moments ago-that the greater part of our public debt was owed to the people in Canada, and I said that at present the payment of the debt and the interest upon it meant that we had to tax the people with families, many of the poor people in this country, to extract from them, by every conceivable device that can be invented by the Minister of Finance, this money to turn it over to a few, many of whom are comparatively wealthy. Would you say that nc matter what happens that debt is a prior claim to the needs of those people?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the money was needed it was very essential that it should come from some source so that the war could be carried on, and I suppose the people who put their money into victory bonds at that time did so in good faith, I would say that the country should stand behind its obligations to these people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like to
call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that the war had to be carried on; there was a lot of men needed to carry on that war, and what did the government do? They went into the homes of people all over the countiy, took out individuals and told them to go to the front, and I urge that if it is right to conscript men, it is right to conscript money. The men were conscripted; the wealth was not conscripted.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wealth should have been conscripted, and do you mean to tell me that we have no right to so adjust our taxation that it will bear heavily on those whose wealth should have been conscripted and was not.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It should have
been conscripted at that time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Do you mean to
tell me that we ought to refuse to adjust our taxation so as to bear heavily upon those who have wealth? I would like to think that the

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
hon. gentleman is a good Liberal. If he were, I think he would be behind me in that. On the whole, the majority, whether on .the Liberal or on the Conservative side, are somewhat inclined to regard wealth as sacrosanct, and if there is not enough to go around the interest charges have to be paid whether men and women suffer or not. I am simply going so far as to say that we should provide for the men, and women and children first. Afterwards if there is enough to go round we should attend to the other obligations.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that when
the matter was being discussed in parliament Sir Robert Borden made the statement, and gave his word to the labour people and others in Canada, that if conscription of men were forced in Canada wealth would also be conscripted?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not prepared to say whether that statement was made or not. I know there was a very general impression that it would not be the common people that would be loaded down with the war debt after the war was over. There was a general impression, too, that after the war we were going to have a large measure of reconstruction so that the mass of the people would be placed on a different footing.
Let me give this other quotation from the article to which I have referred, because it seems to me to indicate so well the point of view of a large number of people all over the country. Referring again to the situation in Great Britain it says:
Two governments are functioning in London at the present time. One of these governments which is now acting on the defensive is the politically representative ministry of Premier Stanley Baldwin, and the other is the industrially representative general council of the Trades Union Congress.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the writer should have gone further. He has omitted the most important government of all, the third government. The third government is the financially representative government of the landowners and the bankers which throughout the years has largely dominated the political government of Great Britain. That dominance is challenged. I am not suggesting that the method of making the challenge is a good method, I am not at the moment passing any opinion with regard to that. But I will say that throughout the history of England, and especially in recent years, the financial control has been so great that there has come a shifting of power gradually from the old feudal land owners to those who have control of the financial system of the country. And they have, to no small extent, controlled the
policies of parliament and control them today; and to-day the labour people-through political action during the last few years, and now through industrial action, whether this is advisedly undertaken or not-are challenging that dominance and are saying in regard to the mines over there that if profits can be paid only by lowering the standards of the people of England, such a condition must not continue; the standards of the people must be maintained even though it means a reorganization of the whole mining industry of the country. That is what lies behind the struggle over there, and that is what we have to consider here in this country.
When we are faced with a budget of this kind and are told that we control less than forty per cent of our expenditures, that the greater part of the taxes we raise are raised by indirect taxation which bears heavily upon the mass of the people, we encounter this very selfsame problem here in this country. Although labour and the farmers are undoubtedly not yet politically strong in Canada, we come challenging the dominance of the financial masters of this country. Members of the older parties have come here from year to year, from decade to decade, and have advocated the policies very largely of the manufacturers, of the big transportation interests, and of the big financial interests. And when anyone dares to question the ideals and policies of these great interests he is ridiculed, and is told that, he is talking wildly, or that he is talking all sorts of academic stuff. I want to say that although it may not suit the ideas of certain gentlemen in .this House, there is a rising tide of public opinion much along the lines that I have been trying to indicate to-night; and I am quite sure that in the days to come we will find more and more the mass of the people asking questions with reference to the reorganization, or, as it was called in immediate post-war days, the "reconstruction", of our industrial and financial system. If we are to go on year by year with a comparatively small group enjoying the prosperity so glowingly referred to in the Governor General's speech, while a large number of .the people are quite unconscious that prosperity has yet arrived, are we not undermining those institutions of parliament which we have said should foe supreme? After all in a democratic country parliament has a right to govern only so far as parliament represents the ideals of the masses of the people of that country.
The Budget-Mr. Tummon

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not having taken part in any of the debates so far, perhaps I might be permitted to make a few observations at this time. In so doing I do not purpose to detain the House at length.
May I briefly summarize recent events in regard to this government? In his Richmond Hill address of September 7th last year, the Prime Minister complained very bitterly that having only a majority of one, he was unable to successfully carry on, and seemingly intimated that unless he obtained a substantial majority he would resign. The country defeated the Prime Minister and eight of his cabinet ministers, and reduced his following in this House to 101. It also decreased the parliamentary representation of the Progressive party from 65 to 24. On the other hand the Conservative party was returned with 116 supporters, an increase of 69. But the government did not resign. The Prime Minister then said he would call parliament and allow the people's representatives to decide who should carry on. A statement to that effect was issued by the Prime Minister and appeared in the press on November 5 last. Parliament was called on January 7 but not for the purpose indicated. It was called to permit the government, through the Speech from the Throne, to present a programme to this House whereby they 'hoped to obtain here what the country refused them on October 29th. In the Speech from the Throne the government declared among other things:
-that in the interest of industrial development every effort should be made to eliminate the element of uncertainty with respect to tariff changes; that changes in the tariff should be made only after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries and that representations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications to advise the ministry with respect thereto. A Tariff Advisory Board will accordingly be appointed forthwith.
That was part of the programme upon which this government obtained the necessary vote3 to permit them to carry on and remain upon the treasury benches. It was thus a surprise to many when the Minister of Finance, in presenting his budget, announced the tariff reduction on automobiles, and only eight days after the Tariff Advisory Board had been appointed. Thus to my mind the situation, is that the government, in order to obtain a majority in the vote on the Speech from the Throne, declared one thing; then, having obtained that majority, proceeded to do an-

other. On the other hand, it has been said that my hon. friends to my left are responsible for the tariff reduction on automobiles. It seems to me that they then, would be in the position of giving their support to the government on one policy, and, having sustained them in power, are demanding another policy. As to who might be responsible I am not concerned. But the result is to have the very opposite effect to that sentence in the Speech from the Throne, which says:
That in the interests of industrial development every effort should be made to eliminate the element of uncertainty with respect to tariff changes.
Thus instead of tending towards the elimination of uncertainty the course of the government has and is increasing the element of uncertainty that ivas already prevailing, As to whether or not the automobile industry was enjoying too much protection I am not prepared to say. I do not feel that I am competent to judge. So far as I can see it would perhaps make little difference to manufacturers of automobiles whether they manufactured in Canada or in the United States. I believe the Canadian plants are most all, if not all, branches of American firms. But it wrould make a great deal of difference to the Dominion of Canada if we should lose that industry! and it does mean much to the thousands of workmen and their families who are dependent upon that industry for a living, many of whom no doubt felt that they were engaged in a legitimate business and that their jobs were secured; and they probably purchased homes and assumed other obligations which to them were comparatively as great as the obligations that the company which employed them assumed in the carrying on of their business. While I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there may be certain difficulties, yet with all due respect to the time honoured custom of keeping the contents of the budget a secret, not revealing them until their presentation to parliament, and then announcing drastic changes such as the one I have referred to, to take effect immediately, with a resulting tendency to demoralize and disrupt-legitimate business and create uncertainty and distrust in the mind of the workman as to his ability to retain his job or to find employment, it seems to me it is wrong and damaging. There were many in Canada who looked forward expectantly to the appointment of a tariff board which they hoped would overcome this difficulty, but their hopes have been shattered when even the government seemingly would not trust its own child. My complaint against this government is that although such a board was created prior to the introduction

The Budget-Mr. Tummon
of the budget, the government ignored its own creation and failed at the first opportunity to fulfil its promise in the Speech from the Throne, that-
-this board will be expected to make a careful study of the customs tariff, the revenue to be derived therefrom and tihe effect of the tariff and allied factors on industry and agriculture.
In regard to the income tax I have only one observation to make, and it refers to the proposed increased exemption. I notice that in discussing this tax two or three different expressions have been used. First, it has been said that the increased exemption will be $3,000 for married men; again it has been stated that the exemption will apply to the heads of families, and again that it will apply to householders. Upon reflection it will be seen that each of these phrases means something different. "Married man" may mean just simply what it saysi-married, perhaps not iiving with his wife, without a family, house, or anything else, and he would get the benefit of the expression. "Householder" means the owner and holder of a house, but the head of a family would mean the possessor of a home who was maintaining therein a wife or housekeeper, and children of his own or children whom he may be keeping as a matter of charity. As the head of a family he would comply with all the requirements, and I consider the increased exemption should apply to that class. I have now in my mind more than one example, but will just mention one to illustrate the point. A widower had a son who met with an accident and died, the son leaving a wife and three children. The daughter-in-law is the 'housekeeper for the father-in-law, and the latter is keeping and providing for the daughter-in-law and grandchildren as if they were his own. The father-in-law should therefore be entitled to the exemption. I think the exemption should apply to the head of a family maintaining a home, a wife or housekeeper and any children solely maintained therein by him.
Coming as I do from a district which was a pioneer in the dairy industry in Canada, a district which can not only lay claim to being a pioneer but also to being one of the leading dairy districts of Canada, where every farmer is practically a dairy farmer, it naturally follows that we are intensely interested in anything that relates to that industry. I propose to refer briefly to the Australian and New Zealand treaties. I have listened while the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), and I think the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) quoted the price of butter on the Montreal market 14011-208
during the winter months, for the purpose of showing that notwithstanding these treaties, and the fact that butter was coming into Canada at the time in large quantities, the price of butter in Canada remained at a high figure. I noticed that the ministers confined their quotations largely, if not wholly, to the one market. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that at a time when the home consumption equals or exceeds the home production, no one market or place is a true gauge of the general price of butter in all other places. I have seen in the winter months in my constituency which is fairly compact, comprising a territory perhaps thirty miles long by an average of fifteen or sixteen miles wide, five or six different prices varying from two to sometimes ten cents per pound according to conditions that exist in each small centre and according to supply and demand.
I also saw a shipment of foreign butter come into one of those small centres during the past winter, and as a result the price of butter fat to the producer immediately dropped because in every case the foreign product was offered at a less price than that of the home product.
For many years both the federal and provincial departments of Agriculture have been urging increased production upon the dairy farmer. I can well remember a number of yeaTS ago the hon. member who sits upon the government side of this House for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) touring our county as a lecturer of the old Farmers' Institute. One of the favourite subjects of those gentlemen in those days was increased production of the daily cow. Anyone who is at all familiar with the handling of dairy cattle knows that some of the ways in which this can be accomplished is by doing away with the culls, by better care, better feeding and better housing but one of the most effective ways is by increasing the lactation period.
In those days-and I refer to eighteen or twenty years ago-dairying was confined almost wholly to the production of cheese. Cheese factories started operations about May 1 and ceased operations about October 31. The farmer's wife after the closing of the cheese factory was able to dispose, at the local market or at the country store, of a couple of churnings of butter; she would then pack sufficient to keep the family supplied during the winter months, and the cows were allowed to cease milking about December 1.
Going back we find that in 1900 Ontario produced only 7.559,542 pounds of creamery butter. Eighteen years ago there were less than half a dozen creameries between the city



The Budget-Mr. Tummon
of Toronto and the Ottawa river: there was at that time little encouragement for the farmer to increase the lactation period of his animals because he could not profitably dispose of his product. I can remember when the first can of sweet milk was shipped from the Belleville district, 120 miles east of Toronto, into the city of Toronto. It was shipped about November 1, after the closing of the cheese factory in the fall, and the man who shipped it was looking around for a market whereby he could milk his cattle for a longer period. Other farmers took up the idea; for years thousands of cans of milk went from that district to Toronto, and herds which had previously ceased milking about December 1 were milked on as a rule until the middle or the end of February.
Eventually creameries began to be established .in convenient centres and these supplied the veiy market the farmer required in order to lengthen the milking period of his herd. To-day in that same territory from Toronto to the Ottawa river where eighteen years ago there were onfy five or six creameries, there are operating to-day seventy-five or eighty creameries, and the production of creamery butter in Ontario for 1925 according to the Dairy and Cold Storage branch was more than 60,000,000 pounds, while Canada as a whole produced in that year 180,663,783 pounds of creamery butter of which she exported 26,646,435 pounds. That does not take into consideration dairy butter and we are told by the Dairy and Cold Storage branch that the manufacture of dairy butter in Canada last year was approximately 100,000,000,-pounds. That makes a total of about 280,000,000 pounds of butter of which we exported only 26,646,435 pounds, or in other words, for every pound of butter that we exported last year we consumed in Canada eleven pounds. Where are those who will tell us that the home market does not amount to much?
We are told by officials of the Dairy and Cold Storage branch of the Department of Agriculture:
There is lots of room for a continued increase in Canadian production of dairy products. The world in the past few years has had an increasing demand for butter and cheese. This is quite marked in Great Britain where as yet our (butter sales are only a drop in the bucket. Canadian butter is quoted on the market there for but a few months in the year and our prospects for increased prices would be better could an all-year supply be provided.
It is plain that in a country such as Canada an all-year supply can be provided only by winter dairying. Winter dairying has been steadily increasing as I hhve endeavoured to show, but it means production under the

most difficult and costly conditions and it needs all the encouragement which this or any other government can give it. Yet in face of these things this government enters into treaties with Australia and New Zealand which permit producers of butter and other dairy products, of the Antipodes producing under the most favourable circumstances, to compete in the Canadian market at the very door of the .Canadian producers, producing under the most difficult conditions. This has been and is creating in the mind of the dairy farmer the same feeling of uncertainty and instability about his business that this government has succeeded in creating in the commercial and industrial life of this country. It seems to me that if there is anything we in Canada need more than another it is a sound, settled, fiscal policy that will eliminate the uncertainty that seems to exist everywhere and restore stability and confidence at large, a policy that will proclaim not only to Canadians but to people of other nations that Canada will supply as far as possible the wants of Canadians.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with others in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the splendid budget he has presented to the House? I believe it has been received by the majority of the people of this country as one of the best budgets that have been presented for a great number of years. It is, I believe, what is commonly called throughout Canada a budget of the common people. It indicates a reduction in taxation which I am sure is very favourably received throughout the Dominion.
The removal of the receipt tax is, I believe, also appreciated, while the removal of the sales tax on many articles is a move in the right direction. Then, on Dominion Day we return to the two-cent postage; and last, but not least, there is the lowering in the income tax. I believe the reduction in the income tax will be of great advantage to great masses of the people. I know that in my own constituency, which is a rural one, this reduction is greatly appreciated, especially among the farmers. As you are no doubt aware, Mr. Speaker, the farmer in western Canada has a great many obstacles to fight, such as drought, hail, rust and frost. Over these things he has no control, so that some years he practically has no returns; and of course when his returns are low he escapes the income tax. On the other hand, when in years of large crops, such as the past year, he reaps a large harvest and receives good prices he naturally has to pay an income tax. I have always

The Budget-Mr. Vallance
contended that, so far as western Canada was concerned, the income tax was one of the greatest grievances of our farmers. And it is of western Canada that I speak. I have always held that in deciding upon the income tax as it affects the farmer of the west an average should be struck over a period of years. I have heard it thrown across the floor of the House to the Saskatchewan group that while we have the largest per capita wealth of any province of the Dominion we do not pay the highest per capita taxation. This is easily explained: we have no very rich men in Saskatchewan, our wealth being more evenly distributed.
There are better times ahead of us in spite of the blue ruin talk we hear from the other side, and I believe that the western farmer is beginning to get on his feet again. I had the privilege while travelling in western Canada during the recess of talking to one of the inspectors of a large banking concern in that part of the country, and he told me that whereas at the corresponding period last year it required four men to write the agricultural credits from the city of Regina, at the time he was speaking one man could easily do this work. Of course the chief reason is the fact that we have had a large crop and, coupled therewith, good prices. But while this is true, while we have had a splendid crop and good prices, I fancy that the explanation lies in this, that the farmers themselves have at last begun to have some say in the marketing of their produce.
Referring to the marketing situation in western Canada, I should like for a few moments briefly to outline the operation of the wheat pool. I believe that
10 p.m. with the operation of the wheat pool and the orderly marketing not only of our wheat, but also of all other grains we shall get all there is in it. We have been accused of establishing the wheat pool with a view to forcing up the prices of wheat, but that is entirely wrong; the pool was organized to control the flow of wheat to the market. In the old days the bulk of our grain was in the hands of speculators, three months after it has been threshed, whereas under the pool we are selling wheat all the time. In this way the market is kept steady, but under the present system the payments are extended over a period of time; we have one initial, and three interim payments, each one coming when the farmer most needs the money. You may ask any banker or mortage or machine company, and they will all tell you the same story, that under this system of marketing the farmer is meeting his obligations better all the time.
HOI 1-208j
Since coming to this House I have heard a good deal of talk about protecting the farmer. Now we western farmers believe that it is utterly impossible to protect us as wheat growers. We have to the south of us a country which it is agreed is one of the most highly protected nations in the world, and what do we find? I have here a review of an article entitled The Plight of the Farmer. It is taken from The Nation, New York, the author being Mr. Smith W. Brookhart, one of the United States senators for Iowa. Senator Brookhart is of the farmers' bloc and is one of the ablest American Progressives. That is what he has to say:
"In the last five years," he begins by saying, "more than a million farmers have become bankrupt, and the value of farm /property has decreased by twenty or twenty-five billions of dollars." Senator Brookhart is speaking of farmers and farm property in the United States. There are many reasons to accept his statement as accurate. Bank failures in the farm states, statistics of rural depopulation and the insistence of farmer politicians on measures of "relief" for agriculture are all evidence that the past few years have seen a decline in the prosperity of American farming.
In the last five years in Canada thousands of farmers have regained financial soundness and the value of farm property has increased iby millions.
Senator Brookhart cites some facts which explain this difference. The causes of the farmer's plight, he writes, "lie for the most part in discrimination against agriculture in the laws that have been enacted for the benefit and protection of business." There is, he says, an enormous discrimination against farmers in transportation. They must pay freight to get their products to market. When they buy the things they need, freight is included in the price. The same situation obtains in Canada, but rates on farm products are veiy much lower here than in the United States.
Another discrimination noted by Senator Brookhart is in tariff legislation. The great manufacturing industries, protected against all competition, fix the price of their product. The price of farm products, on the other hand, is fixed by what can be got for the exportable surplus. The farmer sells in an open market and buys in a closed one. Once again, the position is the same in Canada but the handicap against fanners in the Dominion is not nearly so great.
Senator Brookhart proceeds to suggest a remedy for the farmer's economic distress. His proposals are less interesting to Canadians than the prospect that the plight of agriculture in the United States may drive many American farmers north into this country.
They can buy land much cheaper here than south of the line. With the same amount of work it will produce just as many bushels per acre as land in Minnesota or Kansas. Perhaps it will produce more and the quality of the grain will be superior.
It costs less per acre or per bushel to sow and reap a crop in Canada than in the United States.
I want you to pay particular attention to this:
It costs less to ship grain here. Freight rates are lower now in the Dominion and with the completion of the Hudson Bay railway farmers in the prairie provinces will have open to them the best of all routes from the heart of America to Europe.
All that stands in the way of a land movement northward on this continent is the natural disinclination of settled farmers to migrate.

The Budget-Mr. Vallance
That is the plight of the highly protected American farmer, and yet hon. members opposite would like to protect the wheat grower of western Canada. I wonder if they ever think of the time during the war when they were on the treasury benches, and the protection they gave to the farmers at that time. I wonder if it was to protect the farmer that they set the price of wheat when it started to go up in 1917, and whether it was to protect the farmer after the war, when prices started to tumble, that they ceased to control the market. These are questions which quite naturally arise in the minds of practical farmers.
That brings me to another phase of agriculture which I would like to bring to the attention of the House, and that is the cattle industry. I must congratulate the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) for the persistency with which he has kept this question before the House. I do not think any line of agriculture has suffered more since the war than has the cattle industry. We all remember that in 1917 and 1918 we were being advised to go into the cattle business; credit was easy, and the bankers were advising the farmers to borrow money and buy cattle. Many of us did so; cows were bought at from S100 to $150 per head in 1917, and by 1920 the price had fallen to $35 per head; thousands of farmers were ruined. These are plain facts, as every farmer in this House knows, and it is for these men I desire to plead. What we need most is markets, and this is where I do not quite agree with the hon. member for Marquette. I have here an article taken from the Farm and Ranch Review of December 10, 1925. As I remember the words of the hon. member for Marquette, on the two or three occasions when we dealt with the cattle industry, he was somewhat opposed to the development of the market in the United States, and on that point I wish to take issue with him.
