speechtext:
No one in this House
knows the extent of the Old Country market better than I do. I lived there until I was twenty-one years of age, and I know the type of cattle the Old Country feeder wants. There are many years in western Canada when we have thousands of cattle which

would not pay for shipment to even Winnipeg, and it is almost impossible to find a market in the Old Country for such cattle. I think it was Shakespeare who said:
There is a tide in the affairs of men,
Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.
I believe our tide has now arrived, and it is up to this government and the people of this country to do whatever can be done to remove this injustice and allow our cattle to enter the United States market. The article says:
The psychological moment has arrived when we can appeal to Washington with arguments of commercial self-interest. An enormous com crop has been harvested an the middle west this year. Carter Field, in the New York Herald-Tribune, sizes up the situation as follows:
"With a three-billion-bushel corn crop being dumped on a market Which had been expecting to absorb a two-and-a-half-billion-boishel crop, and with the price of corn on the farm as a result reduced to fifty cents a bushel, President Coolidge has sent two experts to the middle west to see what can be done to save the situation."
Later the article goes on to say:
"The chief trouble is that the corn raisers of this country have piled up a crop estimated at 3,000,000,000 bushels, as against a crop last year of slightly less than 2,500,000,000 bushels. This 20 per cent increase of production naturally would have a tremendously depressing effect on the price, even if there were no other complications.
"Added to this, it is pointed out, is the fact that the number of feeders is much smaller than expected and consequently there is not the normal supply of cattle and hogs which can be fattened on corn..
"The third factor in depressing the price is the fact that the farmers never have fully recovered from the hard times which followed the war. As a result they are not able financially to hold their corn until the natural demand for it increases, but feel obliged to dump it on the market regardless of what they get for it.
"So corn, which they claim cost seventy-five cents a bushel to produce, is being sold on the farms at fifty cents a bushel."
We are told here that one of the difficulties facing the middle west feeder in disposing of his present unprofitable corn crop is that he has not available the normal volume of feeder cattle to enable him to turn his cheap corn into beef. On this point, the Kansas City Star says:
"More than 80 per cent of the corn raised on the farm is marketed on the hoof. The farmer who has plenty of animals on his place feeds his corn to his cattle and hogs. So the price doesn't so much matter. He sells his corn, not as corn, but as beef and pork. So long as he gets a fair price for his finished product, he doesn't worry over the cheapness of the raw material that goes to making that product. It is when a farmer has to buy high-priced corn to feed low-priced animals that he is in trouble."
Canada is irrevocably wedded to a live cattle export trade, and deprived of the United States market we cannot succeed. This is the unvarnished truth. I can readily see, Mr. Speaker, why the hon. member for Marquette would not be in favour of shipping

The Budget-Mr. Vallance
these live cattle to the United States. He and I differ somewhat, I as a breeder and he as a feeder. Towards the end of July and August, if one of those dry summers which quite frequently comes to the west, is prevalent, pasture gets scarce and we naturally have to get rid of a certain percentage of our cattle. It is then that such men as the hon. member for Marquette step up on the Winnipeg market and buy these cattle for what they care to pay. If I were at home I believe I could show a cheque for $1 from a commission house in Winnipeg, for a cattle beast; they will not even pay the freight. Not only do they get cattle at their own prices on the Winnipeg market, but they hold them until we start to ship out our wheat, and with the wheat, we ship the feed with which they fatten these cattle. We even have to pay the freight, We have in that western country one of the greatest cattle raising areas Under the sun. The grass that grows there can bring cattle into the very best feeder condition. All we need is more and wider markets, and I believe the market to the south of us is the best market we can have for this class of cattle. I leave this subject, Mr. Speaker, for the consideration of the House, and I hope that when the resolution of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) comes up asking for a special committee to examine into the whole cattle industry in this country, these conditions I have pointed out will not be overlooked.
They talk about protecting the farmer. I would like to cite a few figures showing just what real protection the American farmer gets with his 42 cents tariff on wheat. In the crop year of 1924-25 there was a tariff of 42 cents on Canadian wheat going into the United States. Yet from August of 1924 until July of 1925 we had a higher average price in Canada. The average price at Winnipeg during that period was 1,685, and at Minneapolis for the same period, 1,675. "Vet they tell us they would protect the farmer by a tariff! These figures prove that any commodity of which you have an exportable surplus cannot be protected, and you must take the price on the world's market.
I notice that quite a number of hon. members opposite from eastern Canada have been advising us westerners to quit growing wheat; for instance, the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) and the hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Baker). Mr. Speaker, I have been growing wheat in Saskatchewan for the last twenty years, and like the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) who sits behind me, I have never grown it when I could not sell it. Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in regard to the duty on automobiles. I expressed my views on this subject on a former occasion when a resolution advocating a reduction in the duty was being considered. But I received a letter the other day, and I thought that if I had the privilege of speaking during the present debate I would bring it to the attention of the House. There are still in western Canada a great many outlying districts remote from railway communication, and the letter in question ilustrates the difficulties from which the settlers in such districts suffer. The 'etter is as follows:
Dear Sir:
The Big Gully Development Association present compliments, and beg your interest in the urging of the build ng of a branch railway line between the north Saskatchewan river and the Big Gully creek.
Many of us have spent almost twenty years in opening up this district and establishing homes, and are still upwards of thirty miles from a railway, which means that practically one-third of our working time is spent on the winter trails.
When we settled in this place it was with the distinct understanding that a line would be built long before this.
At, the time that the average citizen is closing up his business for the day, we start out on the twenty-five mile return trip through the darkness and western cold, which has to be experienced to be understood. This travelling over the everlasting trails is not profitable to us, nor to the country, neither does it become more pleasant with the passing years.
We respectively request your influence with the powers that be to see that this heavy and unfair burden is lifted in the near future.
It is of people such as the writer of the foregoing letter that I am thinking in connection with the duty on automobiles. I doubt whether many of them have reached the state of affluence that would permit them

to buy an automobile, but if it is at all within their power it would prove an immense boon to them. They would be able to transport their wheat by motor truck instead of hauling it long distances by team. It has been figured that we can farm at a distance of twenty-five miles from the railway if we can have the use of a motor truck. The average one-ton truck will travel at the rate of twenty miles an hour but even if it did not cover more than fifteen miles, it would be a great convenience to people who live at such a distance from the shipping point as I have indicated. There are in Saskatchewan many districts such as the writer of the letter indicates. It is of people so circumstanced that the average Saskatchewan member thinks when the duty on automobiles comes up for consideration rather than of persons engaged in the industry, more especially when we consider the enormous profits the industry has yielded to the manufacturers.
I do not wish to occupy any more of the time of the House, but in closing I desire to say this:	In spite of all the blue ruin talk
from hon. gentlemen opposite the facts disclose that Canada has prospered under the present government. With a budget of the kind brought down on April 15 last, coupled with the legislative programme submitted for our approval, there is not much danger but that Canada will continue to forge ahead and enjoy even better times in the future.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to occupy very much of the time of the House to-night, but I feel it incumbent upon me to make a few remarks upon the budget, and also to deal briefly with some of the problems which are confronting the country at the present time.
At the outset may I be allowed to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in which he spoke of the delegation which waited on the government some two weeks ago with regard to the cut in the duty on automobiles. The hon. gentleman stated that the members of that delegation did not represent organized labour, in fact, to use his own words, that the large delegation had been marshalled by the employers in the towns from which the representatives came. I believe the large delegation in question represents labour more truly than does the hon. gentleman himself. They represented the 25,000 people engaged in the automobile industries in Canada, and the 100,000 women and children dependent upon those industries. In corroboration of that statement I will read from the Labour Leader, Canada's national labour weekly, published in Toronto,

The Budget-Mr. Hay
and dated April 23rd, 1926, an appeal to the members of the House of Commons to the following effect:
An appeal to the members of the House of Commons of Canada.
Representing, as you do, the citizens of this great Dominion, the Labour Leader on behalf of the men who work in the Canadian automobile factories and the various factories that make parts and accessories, numbering about twenty-five thousand, with about one hundred thousand women and children dependent upon them, earnestly request you to refer the clause in the budget that deals with the tariff on motor cars to the new tariff commission, so that these workers may have an opportunity of placing their views before them. Gerutlemen, forget your political parties, and lend a hand to these hardworking toiJers.
There is another article along the same line in tfhe Labour Leader but I will not take up time by reading it at present. Yet in the face of articles of that kind, coming from the official organ of the Labour party in Canada, the hon. gentleman in question has the temerity to stand up here and say those people did not represent organized labour.
I desire to refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) when he was speaking on the budget a few days ago. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) a short time ago gave an interview to a Star reporter in Toronto, and I desire to place the report of that interview on Hansard, because I want the people of my constituency at any rate and the people of western Canada to know where that hon. member stands. In the last election six Conservatives were returned from Manitoba, and having regard to the traditional Views of that, province on the tariff, it was thought that with the exception of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen they would act as a brake on the wheel of the Conservative protectionist chariot.
The Budget-Mr. Hay

Then it goes on to say:
Careful reading of Hansard will show that all of the Manitoba Conservatives have defined their positions with the exception of Thomas Hay of Springfield, and T. G. Murphy of Neepawa, who have bravely declined so far all opportunities to speak, and who are indeed the only bushel covered lights remaining in the opposition so far.
In reply to that article I have only this to say, that so far as the principle of protection is concerned I believe in it. I am a protectionist and believe that protection is the only policy that will make Canada a prosperous country. Whilst almost every other country in the civilized world to-day is raising her tariff and protecting the industries and the home market, some Canadians are the only ones to-day who are preaching free trade in the face of what is happening in the world, and I cannot understand how the doctrine of free trade can be preached when all other countries are preaching and practising protection,. The Free Press need have no doubts as to where I stand so far as protection is concerned. I believe in a protective policy and I preached that policy from every platform in my constituency during the last campaign. I believe in a policy of protection that will, first of all, protect our Canadian industries, that will protect our Canadian workingman, that will protect their jobs and protect our natural resources; a policy of protection that will protect the Canadian farmer as well and protect and build up his home market.
I wish to refer to a speech made by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) during the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. That hon. member declared himself to be a free trader. Mr. Michael Clark was accounted as the apostle of free trade in this country for some years; his mantle must have fallen upon the shoulders of the hon. member for Rosetown. That hon. member is a reformer, and I believe a reformer of the destructive type, as I will try to show in the course of my remarks. Some hon. members on my extreme left laugh, but I think after I get through they will conclude that I am absolutely correct in what I say. That remark applies to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail). I think these hon. members can all be included in the one class.
The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), speaking on the tariff during the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, said that he believed in free

trade. He said further at that time, speaking of our industrial institutions, that they were built up on hothouse methods and that they must be destroyed, put out of the way. Consequently, I say that the hon. member is of the destructive type, the Carrie Nation type, if I may use the expression. Carrie Nation flourished in the United States a few years ago as a reformer, a reformer too of the destructive type. She used to sally forth with her little axe and destroy everything that came in her way. As regards the hon. member for Rosetown and the others whom I have mentioned, while their little tomahawks are not much in evidence at the present time, I feel that if their policies were put into effect they would be more destructive than Carrie Nation's little axe.
I should like to refer to a speech made by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. How-den) who I am glad is in his seat. It was the hon. member's maiden speech in this House, and while it was well and forcibly delivered I for one cannot agree, and I am sure very few members on this side of the House will agree, with the conclusions arrived at by that hon. gentleman. Speaking of the tariff he said that if it so happened that during the night all the industries from one end of Canada to the other were wiped out of existence, while the country would receive a very rude shock it would eventually recover from that shock and the people engaged in those industries would eventually drift to the land and become producers. That has not been the experience of the Canadian people during the last four years.

I desire to quote from a letter which I received from a gentleman who lives just adjoining the constituency of the hon. member for St. Boniface. He is an old-timer, a descendant of one of the original settlers. He is a man of wide experience who, I think, is well known to the hon. member. This is what he has to say regarding this matter:
If an opportunity affords you in the House our gardeners need protection from especially the early stuff being dumped from the United States so that when our products are ready the price is down to nothing.
Then he says further:
It was one of our members who won a prize at the Royal show, Toronto, last fall with his collection of vegetables.
That is a pretty good recommendation for ths gardeners of Manitoba.
The Progressive party, in advocating certain policies which they have been advocating ever since they first came into this House as a group, such as the policy of free trade and the cutting off of the duty on all agricultural implements, or implements of production, as they generally term it, are in my opinion rather narrow in their outlook. They are somewhat restricted in their vision in advocating such a policy. I suppose they are sincere in their beliefs, and they seem to think that if the policy they propose were put into effect they would be able to buy binders, mowers, ploughs and other agricultural implements cheaper than they can get them to-day. They remind me of the story I used to read as a schoolboy, of the dog which while crossing the brook with a bone in his mouth snatched at the reflection in the water, mistaking it for another and better bone than the one he had. He lost the one he had and found that there was no other. Hon. gentlemen put me in mind of that fable: they are quite ready to grasp at the shadow, taking a chance on losing the substance. They are willing, indeed, to sacrifice other industries in order to advance the interests of their own, failing to see the fallacy that underlies such a policy. That is not a national policy; it is not a policy that should commend itself to the people of the country. In my opinion

The Budget-Mr. Hay
it is a policy which the Canadian people when they have an opportunity will reject.
With regard to the budget and the speech of the Minister of Finance in introducing it, I have no doubt that when placing his annual statement before parliament he really felt that he was offering something that would be satisfactory to the people at large. It seems to me, however, that after it has been analysed and carefully looked into the budget as a whole will not appeal to the people. They will not be quite so enthusiastic about it as the minister and the government evidently assume. It is not such a budget as will appeal to the common people, the labourers of Canada; it will to a greater extent affect the people of means. It may take from such people something more in the way of income tax, and I have no objection to that, because in mj' opinion no man with an income of $5,000 or $10,000 should be reluctant to pay a fair share of taxation. But so far as the poor man is concerned, the budget offers no great relief. The present proposals will not tend to any great extent to relieve the poor people of Canada of the burdens which they are bearing to-day, so that when the government refers to it as the poor man's budget they are misapplying that term. We must however give the Minister of Finance credit for candour in presenting his statement. I admire the rugged honesty he showed in informing the House at the outset that (he reason he was able to submit to the oeople what he considered a satisfactory budget- and he made no bones about it-was because bountiful nature had blessed us with a good crop during the past year. He is quite right in that. It is not by reason of any policy of the government that we are enjoying some measure of prosperity to-day; it is simply because bountiful nature has been kind to us.
When the minister speaks of the prosperity which prevails just now, I want to refer him to an item of news which appeared in the Ottawa Journal some time ago. No doubt he will discount it, seeing the source from which I take it. However, the article in question refers to a statement made by a labour delegate at a meeting held in the city of Ottawa on February 20, I bell p.m.	lieve-the date does not appear
-to the effect that there were in Ottawa at that time over 6,000 men out of employment and that their families were practically facing starvation. Now, I would ask the Minister of Finance whether there is any use in any government or any set of men telling the country that we are prosperous while such a condition of affairs exists.

Could the Minister of Finance possibly convince any one of those 6,000 men that conditions to-day are prosperous? Could he make any one of the hundred thousand men who are out of employment throughout Canada at the present time believe that general prosperity prevails? I say, while he may be sincere he is beside the mark in stating that this Dominion as a whole is prosperous. I appreciate the fact that a measure of prosperity does exist in certain districts, and particularly among the market gardeners and farmers, the men who, my hon. friend from St. Boniface says, would not be hurt if they were deprived of the home market. It is useless to talk about prosperity under present conditions. I certainly do believe that we are on the eve of a great era of progress if only we can secure a sound policy under stab'e government. There is nothing that could stop us unless it were an unstable policy such as the policy now in force, which is undermining public confidence in our institutions and in representative government. Here we have supposed representatives of the people promising at one time to stabilize conditions, and at another, without any warning, introducing such changes as will throw thousands of men out of employment.
I want to refer for a moment or two to some remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) during the debate that occurred on the Australian treaty, as well as during the discussion of other treaties consummated by this government. During the consideration of the Australian treaty protests came in, I think I am safe in saying, from every province in the Dominion, against the unfair competition to which our people would be submitted in consequence of that and other treaties entered into by this government. One or two of those protests I wish to read to the Minister of Agriculture for his information, because at the time, in my opinion, he treated them very lightly,
I have a quotation here from Three Rivers, Quebec, dated February 26, 1926. in connection with which I would like to make some remarks. It says:
A plea for adequate protection for Canadian butter against foreign competition was made this evening by Frank Byrne, of Charlesbourg, first vice-president of the General Breeders' Association of Quebec, at the closing meeting of its thirty-fourth convention.
"If we could produce 15.000,000 pounds of butter more annually." said Mr. Byrne, "we could sell them, but a difficulty arises in the way of success. Other countries threaten to sell their butter here. We ought to hit foreign butter as hard as foreign countries hit our butter. Duties as high as those established bv foreign countries ought to be imposed here, and 1 hope that the government will see to it."

The Budget-Mr. Hay
That is one of the protests which came to the Minister of Agriculture during the discussion of these treaties. With reference to this particular article I would like to say that these people who met in convention in Three Rivers must have represented the Conservative party very largely, because it will be noticed that in the resolution passed by that convention the brick for brick policy denounced by hon. members opposite is advocated. That is the tariff which the Conservative party has been advocating, so far as it relates to the products of the Canadian farmer, and that is the tariff which those people believe in. When our friends opposite from Quebec try to show by figures that .the vote on October 29 last throughout Canada was in some respects favourable to the Liberal party, I want to tell them that the vote in Quebec must have been largely for the policy indicated by this article, the policy advocated by the Conservative party in Canada. We can take no other meaning from the article I have just read.
We had other (protests from the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and particularly from British Columbia. In Manitoba also a resolution was passed somewhat similar to the one passed in Quebec, reading as follows:
That the National Dairy Council appoint a committee to wait on the federal government to urge adjustment of the Australian treaty.
When these protests were coming from all quarters and from almost every province in the Dominion, the Minister of Agriculture insulted the dairying interests by his attitude at that time with respect to their protests; his language was an insult to the dairying interests of Manitoba. When these protests were coming in the minister said that if the dairying interests of Canada would devote more time to improving the quality of their butter rather than to making protests against trade treaties between Canada and Australia, they would do more good. Our butter has a reputation on the markets of the world for quality, Mr. Speaker, and when the. hon. minister makes that statement he is unfair to the dairying interests of the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
I think my hon.
friend is not quite fair. Surely I did not put it in just that way. Has my hon. friend the statement?

speechtext:
The minister went further, and
belittled the dairying interests of this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh no; my hon.
friend goes too far.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He even went so far as to insult the good old Canadian dairy cow as well. He said that the unit of production was the dairy cow, and that if we wished to compete successfully with other countries we must improve the productivity of the dairy cow. In my opinion-and I know something of farming and of cows-the good old Canadian dairy cow has been doing her duty by the people of Canada for many years, but I fail to see that the Minister of Agriculture is doing his duty by the Canadian dairy cow.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Does the hon.
gentleman know the production of milk per cow in Canada?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say the minister is not doing his duty by the Canadian dairy cow, because he is placing her up against an unfair competition from outside sources; he is placing her up against competition that she cannot successfully meet. At a time of the year when our dairy cattle are being housed, with dry feed, it is impossible to meet the competition of the Australian or New Zealand dairy cow which, at that season of the year, is out on the green pasture; when her flow of milk is greater than the flow of milk from the Canadian cow at that season. When the minister speaks of improving the quality of Canadian butter, I want to refer him to a letter received from the External Trade branch of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, dated February 10, 1926. In response to a request for information from this department in connection with the Manitoba dairying interests I received this reply, which is headed, "Dairying in Manitoba." I will only read part of the letter, as I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the House:
Three hundred and fifteen carloads of creamery butter was shipped out of the province of Manitoba last year, or a total of 126,000 fifty-six pound boxes, totalling 7,056,000 pounds valued at $2,416,680. The most of this butter was shipped direct to the British market during the summer months of heavy production, and when the butter was fresh and in the best condition. Manitoba butter has given excellent satisfaction on the British market.
That was from Manitoba alone, a province only in its infancy as regards dairying. Then the letter goes on to state that most of this butter was shipped direct to the British market, during the summer months of heavy production, and that it had given excellent satisfaction there.
It will be seen from that letter that our Canadian creamery butter, particularly, has a
The Budget-Mr. Hay

very high reputation for quality in the markets of the world, and consequently I think it ill becomes the Minister of Agriculture to belittle the quality of that butter.
I should like to give a quotation as to the effect of the Australian trade treaty on the butter situation in Canada. I am sorry that my friends of the Progressive party have deserted the chamber. I was going to say to them that if the statements attributed to the hon. member for Brandon in the interview which he denies were true, they could no longer be called Progressives. I think the term applied to them, and which they resented very much some years ago, could truthfully be applied to them at this time if the statements credited to the hon. member for Brandon were correct; and that term was that the Progressives were but a dilapidated annex of the Liberal party.
I will now give the quotation from the Scoop Shovel, in its issue of April, 1296. This publication is the official organ of the Manitoba Co-operative Wheat Producers Limited and of the Manitoba Pool, and is published in Winnipeg. It says:
Prices of dairy products for the past few months have been very remunerative to the producers, but we arc reaching a stage where we must be prepared to accept lower prices on account of importations of Australian and New Zealand butters, largely due to the more favourable conditions brought about by the action of the government in entering into the Australian treaty which lowered the duty against the entry of Australian butter. Had this butter not been brought in we could have expected a steady market for at least the month of April or until the season of heavy production, when the production of Canadian butter exceeds the consumption.
Coming from such a source, this view should have some weight with the hon. Minister of Agriculture.
It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that some kind of family compact exists between the Liberal party and the Progressives. In that connection I should like to remind my Progressive friends that the Minister of Agriculture, speaking in the town of Selkirk, Manitoba, made the statement that the greatest block on the wheels of progress in this country to-day was the Progressive party. I do not know whether he will deny that or not, but I believe his statement is absolutely correct. While there is evidently some agreement existing between these two groups, some kind of unholy alliance, there is evidently no love lost between them, for I notice that at a Liberal convention at Edmonton in the province of Alberta, held the other day, which was attended by Liberal representatives from all over the province, a gentleman was chosen 
as the provincial Liberal leader by the name of Shaw. I have not the honour of knowing him, but no doubt he stands high in the councils of the Liberal party. I believe that he at one time deserted the Liberal party to which he originally belonged, joined the Progressives, and now after a time has gone back to his first love. Mr. Speaker, his very first act after being chosen leader of the Liberal party in Alberta was to make an attack upon the Progressives of the province of Alberta and upon the Progressives of the Dominion generally. I want to place these words on Hansard because I may have oe-casion to refer to them if I ever go before the electors again. The newspaper report says:
At the afternoon session, Joseph T. Shaw, newly elected leader, launched an attack upon the Farmer government of Alberta, terming it one of inaction.
That describes the attitude of the Progressives, not only in Alberta, but in the Dominion as a whole.
I do not wish to take up very much more time, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion, there is no reason to my mind why Canada should be to-day not merely one of the most prosperous countries of the world, but actually the most prosperous country in the world. With its immense areas of fertile agricultural lands, with its great areas of timber, with its wealth of fisheries, with its vast undeveloped natural resources, with its great possibilities for the production of cheap hydro-electric power, there is no reason why Canada should not be the most prosperous country on the face of the globe. But the fact is, Mr. Speaker, that confidence in this country has been undermined by policies which have been unstable and unsound, and until we put into effect sound and stable policies we cannot expect to have that general prosperity which every Canadian would like to see in this country. Our great natural resources, when properly developed, should make this country the richest in the world. It is estimated that some 19,000,000 horse power of hydro-electric energy can be developed in the Dominion, and I am proud to say that some five or six million of that amount can be developed in the province of Manitoba alone. With a proper policy, this source of energy will make not only Manitoba prosperous, but the Dominion as a whole. It only requires sound and proper policies to develop our great natural resources and make this country the greatest and most prosperous in the world. There is no reason why we should not attain

that happy position. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the House for your kindly attention.
